title: Buying and Selling Property in Washington: What You Are Actually Signing
titleTag: Buying and Selling Property in Washington | Justin D. Leigh
description: What a Washington purchase and sale agreement commits you to, how contingencies and earnest money really work, and what the Form 17 disclosure does not cover.
lede: You signed a purchase and sale agreement eleven days ago, the inspection came back with a page and a half of problems, and your agent says the response deadline is tomorrow. Or you are the seller, you have an offer well over asking, and the buyer waived everything. Either way you are now realizing that the stack of forms you initialed is a binding contract, and you are not entirely sure what it says.
intro: That is a reasonable place to be. Buying and selling property in Washington runs on preprinted forms that are mostly well drafted, and those forms are also where nearly every dispute starts, because the parties sign them without working out what the deadlines and escape hatches actually do.

sections.heading: What does a Washington purchase and sale agreement commit you to?

paras.p: A purchase and sale agreement is an enforceable contract to convey land, and in Washington every conveyance of real estate, along with every contract creating an encumbrance on it, must be by deed. RCW 64.04.010. The agreement is the promise; the deed is the performance. Most of what goes wrong happens in the gap between the two.

The agreement fixes the price, the closing date, who pays which costs, what personal property stays, and the condition of title the seller has to deliver. Preprinted forms generally require title to be marketable, which Washington courts have described as title free of reasonable doubt that a reasonably informed and intelligent purchaser would accept. Marketable does not mean perfect, and it does not mean free of every recorded restriction.

That is where buyers get surprised. A recorded easement across the back of the lot, or a covenant forbidding the shop building you intend to put up, may not make title unmarketable at all. The seller can still be fully entitled to close. The problem belongs to you.

sections.heading: How do contingencies work, and why do deals die there?

paras.p: A contingency makes your obligation to close depend on something happening first. The common ones are financing, a general inspection, review of the title report, and the sale of your current home. Two features matter far more than people expect.

Both sides owe good faith. When both parties accept an agreement containing a contingency, each has a good faith obligation to try to fulfill it. A buyer who simply stops returning the lender's calls is not safely walking away.

The approval standard is not what most people assume. For a contingency to be subject to your approval in your sole discretion, rather than a reasonable discretion standard, the language has to say so specifically. Whether your form says sole discretion or says nothing is the difference between an unreviewable decision and one a court can second-guess.

The financing contingency shows why the drafting matters. Where financing is a true condition precedent to closing and the buyer makes good faith efforts and still cannot obtain the loan, the buyer is not in default, the failure to close is excused, and the earnest money comes back. Restructure that clause and the same buyer, acting identically, forfeits the deposit.

sections.heading: What happens to my earnest money if the deal falls apart?

paras.p: Washington has a statute on this, and it is more specific than most people expect. A provision making forfeiture of the earnest money the seller's sole and exclusive remedy, where a party fails without legal excuse to complete the purchase, is valid and enforceable regardless of whether the seller incurred any actual damages, so long as the amount does not exceed five percent of the purchase price. RCW 64.04.005(1).

Within five percent, the seller keeps the deposit without proving a single dollar of loss. Above five percent the statutory safe harbor simply does not apply, and the clause is interpreted and enforced without regard to the statute, under the common law. RCW 64.04.005(3).

So the size of the deposit relative to the price changes the legal rules governing it. A buyer putting down a large deposit to make an offer competitive is making a legal decision, not only a financial one.

sections.heading: What is the Form 17 seller disclosure statement, and what does it cover?

paras.p: Chapter 64.06 RCW requires the seller of residential real property to deliver a completed disclosure statement, commonly called Form 17, on a form set out in the statute itself. The improved residential form is at RCW 64.06.020 and the unimproved form is at RCW 64.06.015. The statutory forms get revised, and the version printed in the RCW is the one that controls.

The timing is tight. Unless the buyer waived the right to receive it, the seller delivers the statement not later than five business days after mutual acceptance or as otherwise agreed, and the buyer then has three business days, or as otherwise agreed, either to approve it or to rescind the agreement. RCW 64.06.030. If the buyer says nothing in that window, the statement is deemed approved.

The limit on seller liability disappoints people on both sides. A seller is not liable for an error, inaccuracy, or omission in the disclosure statement if the seller had no actual knowledge of it. RCW 64.06.050(1). Form 17 discloses what the seller actually knows. It is not a warranty, it is not an inspection, and a seller who genuinely did not know about the failing drain field has not violated the statute by failing to disclose it.

Several transfers are exempt from the chapter entirely, including foreclosures and deeds in lieu, certain family transfers, and transfers by a personal representative or bankruptcy trustee. RCW 64.06.010. A buyer may also expressly waive receipt, with one carve-out: the buyer cannot waive the Environmental section if the answer to any question in it would be yes. RCW 64.06.010(7).

The statute does not replace your other claims. Nothing in the chapter extinguishes a buyer's existing rights against a seller or a seller's agent under common law, statute, or contract, and nothing in it creates any new remedy beyond the rescission it describes. RCW 64.06.070. Fraudulent concealment, misrepresentation, and in some circumstances a Consumer Protection Act claim against an agent live outside the Act.

sections.heading: What does escrow do, and what happens at closing?

paras.p: Escrow is a neutral third party holding the money and the signed documents until both sides perform. Escrow does not represent you, does not advise you on whether the deal is good, and will not tell you that the easement on the title commitment prevents the use you bought the land for.

Closing ends with recording, and in Spokane County deeds and deeds of trust are recorded with the Spokane County Auditor. Recording is not a formality. An unrecorded conveyance is void as against a later good faith purchaser or mortgagee for value from the same seller whose conveyance is recorded first, and an instrument is deemed recorded the minute it is filed for record. RCW 65.08.070(1). The race to the recorder's office is a real race.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: Buyers who waive contingencies to win a bidding war. In a competitive market the quickest way to make an offer attractive is to delete the protections. That works until the furnace, the roof, or the lender turns out to be a problem, and then there is no contingency to invoke and the earnest money is at risk under a clause the buyer never read. Waiving an inspection is a decision to buy the house in whatever condition it is actually in.

Sellers who shade a Form 17 answer. Because liability turns on actual knowledge, the dangerous answers are not the honest "don't know" ones. They are the ones where the seller knew something, chose a softer answer, and left a paper trail. The disclosure statement is signed, dated, and sitting in the file years later, which is exactly when a buyer's lawyer reads it.

Anyone who signs a form agreement with terms they never read. These forms allocate risk with real precision. Whether approval is in your sole discretion, whether a deadline runs in business days, whether the deposit is above or below five percent, whether financing is a condition precedent or a representation. All of these change the outcome, and none of them announce themselves.

Both sides treating the title commitment as somebody else's job. The exceptions in a title commitment are where easements and recorded restrictions appear, and the window to object is short. That document deserves its own read, which is why I wrote separately about how to read a preliminary title commitment.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here that you cannot do yourself

paras.p: Most of the value is not in drafting from scratch. It is in reading what you are about to sign against what you actually want the property for, and knowing which preprinted terms are negotiable and which are load-bearing.

In practice that means checking whether the contingency language gives you the approval standard you think you have, sizing the deposit with RCW 64.04.005 in mind, reading the title exceptions against your intended use rather than a generic standard of marketability, and calculating the Form 17 and contingency deadlines in business days from the right trigger date. It also means saying plainly when the problem in front of you is a legal problem and when it is a price negotiation, because those get handled differently and confusing them is expensive.

That is the work I do. I am an independent attorney in downtown Spokane, admitted in both Washington and Oregon, which helps on transactions and disputes that straddle the state line. Real estate is the largest part of my practice: residential and land purchase and sale transactions, title and survey review, disclosure disputes, earnest money fights, easement and boundary matters, and quiet title litigation, in Spokane County Superior Court and the surrounding Inland Northwest counties.

title: How to Read a Title Report in Washington: Schedule B Is the Whole Document
titleTag: How to Read a Title Report in Washington | Justin D. Leigh
description: What Schedule A and Schedule B mean, why a title exception is not a defect, and what Washington title insurance does not cover. Read before you object.
lede: Escrow emailed you a forty-page PDF called a Preliminary Commitment for Title Insurance, your agent said it looks clean, and your contract gives you a few days to object to anything in it. Pages four through nine are a numbered list of recorded documents with dates and auditor's file numbers and almost no explanation.
intro: Learning how to read a title report is the highest-return hour a buyer can spend before closing, because that numbered list is where easements, access problems, and recorded use restrictions live. The deadline to raise them is short, and once it passes, those items are yours.

sections.heading: What is a preliminary title commitment, and what is it not?

paras.p: Washington's insurance code answers that directly. A preliminary report, commitment, or binder is a report furnished in connection with an application for title insurance, and it is an offer to issue a title policy subject to the stated exceptions. Then comes the sentence that surprises everyone: the report is not a representation as to the condition of the title to real property, but is a statement of terms and conditions upon which the issuer is willing to issue its title policy, if the offer is accepted. RCW 48.29.010(3)(f).
The commitment does not tell you your title is good. It tells you what the title company is willing to insure and what it refuses to insure.

It is also not an abstract of title. An abstract lists all recorded conveyances, instruments, or documents that impart constructive notice with respect to the chain of title. RCW 48.29.010(3)(a). A commitment is shorter and more selective: the items listed are the ones the title company's examination concluded affect its coverage, not every document of record touching your parcel. The same statute says expressly that preliminary reports are not abstracts and that the duties applicable to preparing an abstract do not apply to them.

That has a practical edge. Something can be recorded against your property, be fully enforceable against you, and still not appear in the commitment, because the title company did not consider it relevant to the risk it was underwriting.

sections.heading: Schedule A versus Schedule B: what each part tells you

paras.p: The current standard form is the 2021 ALTA commitment, built from a Notice, a Commitment to Issue Policy, Commitment Conditions, Schedule A, Schedule B Part I, Schedule B Part II, and a counter-signature. All of those sections must be present for the commitment to be effective.

Schedule A is the identification page: the proposed amount of insurance, the name of the proposed insured, the estate or interest involved, who currently holds title, and the legal description. Read the legal description against what you believe you are buying, and the vesting against the name of the person signing your purchase agreement. Mismatches at this stage are common and fixable; after closing they are neither.

Schedule B, Part I, Requirements lists what must happen before a policy issues, typically an executed deed and mortgage, excise tax forms and payment, payoff information for mortgages being cleared, an owner's affidavit, entity authority documents, and payment of the premium.

Schedule B, Part II, Exceptions is the substance: the matters recorded against title that the title company determined affect its coverage, usually identified by recorded document number. The company ordinarily delivers copies of those instruments along with the commitment, plus the vesting deed and any available tax maps. Those attachments are the actual due diligence material, and the part most buyers never open.
The commitment also expires, commonly six months from its effective date if its conditions are not satisfied.

sections.heading: What does a title exception actually mean?

paras.p: An exception is not an accusation that something is wrong. It is a statement that the insurer will not cover this item. Non-delinquent property taxes, utility easements, plat restrictions, and recorded covenants appear as exceptions in ordinary transactions where nothing has gone wrong.
The useful move is to separate two questions the commitment deliberately blurs.
Does this item cloud ownership? That is a title question, and the one title insurance is designed to answer.
Does this item prevent what I intend to do with the land? That is a use question, and the policy is largely indifferent to it.

A recorded covenant limiting the parcel to one single-family residence is a perfectly ordinary exception. It is not a title defect. It is also fatal to a buyer who bought the lot to build a duplex, and the title company has no obligation to mention that, because the restriction is disclosed and excepted exactly as the form contemplates.

Recorded easements work the same way. An easement appearing as an exception tells you a document exists. It does not tell you where on your land it runs, how wide it is, who may use it, or who maintains it. Those answers live in the recorded instrument and sometimes only in a survey, and the difference can be the difference between a driveway and a lawsuit. I wrote separately about easements and boundary disputes, because scope is where those matters are won.

sections.heading: What are the standard exceptions, and why do they matter?

paras.p: Exceptions come in two kinds. Special exceptions are specific to your property, appear in the public records, and carry a recording number. Standard exceptions are specific to nothing; they appear verbatim in every commitment and describe risks no record search can find.
In Washington the four standard exceptions commonly seen are:
rights or claims of parties in possession not shown by the public records;
encroachments, encumbrances, and other matters adversely affecting title that would be disclosed by an accurate survey of the land;
easements, prescriptive rights, and rights-of-way not shown by the public records; and
mechanics' lien claims not shown by the public records.

Read those four together and you have an honest list of what a standard policy leaves on your side of the line. That list reaches an unrecorded driveway easement a neighbor has used for twenty years, a fence eight feet onto your lot, a contractor who has not been paid, and a tenant nobody mentioned.

A policy leaving those in place is standard coverage. An extended coverage policy insures against them by deletion: the exceptions are raised in the commitment and then intentionally removed from the final policy. Title companies generally underwrite that by requiring a seller's affidavit of title and a current ALTA/NSPS Land Title Survey, and they charge a surcharge. Whether to buy extended coverage, and who pays, is negotiable, and most residential buyers never learn it was available.

sections.heading: What does title insurance actually insure?

paras.p: A title policy is a contract of indemnity, paid for with a single premium, and its coverage is retrospective rather than prospective. It insures against things that already happened before the Date of Policy, which is when the insured acquired its interest, and under current forms that date is generally the outside limit of coverage. The core coverages carried into the 2021 forms protect against title vesting other than as stated in Schedule A, any defect, lien, or encumbrance on title, unmarketability of title, and lack of a right of access to and from the land.

What it does not insure matters just as much. Exclusion 1.a. of the current forms excludes coverage for any law or governmental regulation that regulates, restricts, or prohibits the use and occupancy of the land, the character, dimensions, or location of any improvement, a subdivision of the land, or environmental remediation or protection. Zoning, building codes, setbacks, short-plat eligibility, critical-areas rules, and septic permitting are, with narrow exceptions, outside the policy. The forms reinforce this by defining Public Records as the recording system that imparts constructive notice, expressly excluding building, zoning, planning, licensing, health, public safety, and environmental protection records.
So the policy will not tell you whether you can build, or whether the existing garage was permitted. And anything listed in Schedule B is, by definition, not covered.

sections.heading: Owner's policy or lender's policy?

paras.p: Two policies normally issue in a financed purchase, and buyers routinely confuse them. Both cover proper vesting, absence of title defects, marketability, and access, and the lender's policy adds coverage specific to the mortgage, including the validity and priority of the lien.

But the insured under a lender's policy is the lender. An insured owner can recover its actual monetary loss when a covered matter causes damage; an insured lender generally accrues a right of recovery only after declaring a default, accelerating the debt, and acquiring title, which makes a loan policy claim much less likely to be paid. Paying for the lender's policy at closing buys you nothing. If you want coverage for yourself, you buy an owner's policy.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: The buyer who never opens Schedule B. This is the ordinary case and the costly one. The commitment arrives, the objection window runs, closing happens. Two years later the owner learns the recorded access easement serving the parcel crosses land the seller never owned, or that the covenant at exception 7 prohibits the use the property was bought for. Neither is a title defect, and neither is covered.

Treating an exception as a description. An exception identifies a document. Where the easement lies, how wide it is, and whether the gravel road you drove in on is even inside it are questions a legal description and a survey answer.

Buying standard coverage without a survey. The survey exception and the unrecorded-easement exception are precisely the two problems that become neighbor litigation. Declining both the survey and the extended coverage leaves no one carrying that risk except you.
Assuming silence means safety. A commitment is selective by design. An item can be absent from Schedule B and still bind you.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here that you cannot do yourself

paras.p: Reading a title report well is less about insurance law than about reading the underlying recorded documents against a specific plan for the property. The commitment flags that a document exists; the work is pulling it, reading its legal description, locating it on the ground, and deciding whether it matters to you.

In practice that means separating boilerplate exceptions from substantive ones, reading the easement and covenant instruments rather than their one-line summaries, confirming the insured legal description matches the parcel and that access to a public road is actually insured, deciding whether extended coverage and a survey are worth their cost, and drafting a title objection that preserves your position before the contractual window closes. It also means saying when an exception is a genuine problem and when it is the ordinary furniture of a recorded chain of title, because treating every exception as an emergency is its own expensive mistake.

That is the work I do. I am an independent attorney in downtown Spokane, and real estate is the largest part of my practice. Title and survey review is routine in it, both for parties in a pending transaction and for owners who found the problem afterward. I also handle easement and access disputes, boundary and encroachment matters, and quiet title actions in Spokane County Superior Court and the surrounding Inland Northwest counties. Instruments for property in this county are recorded with the Spokane County Auditor.

title: Adverse Possession in Washington: Ten Years, Five Elements, and Why Mowing Is Not Enough
titleTag: Adverse Possession in Washington State | Justin D. Leigh
description: What Washington requires to claim land by adverse possession, how permission destroys a claim, and why a prescriptive easement is a different thing.
lede: Your neighbor's fence has been eight feet onto your lot since before you bought the place, and he has just told you the strip is his because he has maintained it for fifteen years. Or you are the one who has mowed, graveled, and parked on that strip for a decade, and the new owner next door has staked a survey line through the middle of your garden.
intro: Adverse possession in Washington is an unusually tidy doctrine to state and an unusually difficult one to apply. The elements fit in one sentence. Whether a given set of facts satisfies them has produced a century of litigation, and the answer turns on details neither neighbor thinks to notice.

sections.heading: What does Washington require to prove adverse possession?

paras.p: The elements come from case law rather than a single statute. To establish a claim of adverse possession, the possession must be exclusive, actual and uninterrupted, open and notorious, and hostile and under a claim of right made in good faith.

The clock comes from a statute, and not the one people expect. The period throughout which these elements must concurrently exist is ten years, under RCW 4.16.020, which sets a ten-year limitation period for actions for the recovery of real property. Chaplin, 100 Wn.2d at 857. Chapter 7.28 RCW supplies related provisions, including the shorter alternatives below, but the ordinary ten-year route runs through RCW 4.16.020.
Two features matter more than the rest.

First, the elements must exist concurrently and for the full ten years. Nine years of perfect possession followed by a year of absence does not add up. The claimant also carries the burden on every element, because the legal title holder enjoys the presumption of possession.

Second, "hostile" does not mean hostile. Washington abandoned any requirement of subjective bad intent decades ago. The nature of the possession is determined solely on the basis of the manner in which the possessor treats the property, and the possessor's subjective belief about who really owns the land is irrelevant. Chaplin, 100 Wn.2d at 861. A neighbor who sincerely believed the fence was the boundary is not disqualified by that belief, and one who knew better does not lose for knowing.

sections.heading: What kind of use is enough?

paras.p: This is the question the elements do not answer, and where most claims fail.

The measure is not effort, and not duration alone. The ultimate test is the exercise of dominion over the land in a manner consistent with actions a true owner would take. What counts depends on the land. Washington courts hold that what constitutes adverse possession of a particular tract depends on the nature, character, and locality of the land and the uses to which land of that type is ordinarily put. Possession sufficient for a timbered rural parcel looks nothing like possession sufficient for a city lot.

So the honest answer to "is mowing enough?" is that it depends on what an owner of that strip would ordinarily do with it. Mowing a lawn strip in a platted neighborhood, together with planting, fencing, parking, and treating the area as part of the yard for ten unbroken years, is the pattern that has succeeded. Mowing alone, on land where mowing is what a courteous neighbor does anyway, is the pattern that fails.

sections.heading: How does permission destroy an adverse possession claim?

paras.p: Completely, and this is the most common reason a claim collapses. Permission to occupy the land, given by the true title owner to the claimant or his predecessors in interest, will still operate to negate the element of hostility. Chaplin, 100 Wn.2d at 861 to 862. Permission and adversity are mutually exclusive, so if the use began with consent, the clock never started.
Two consequences follow that people find counterintuitive.

A handshake with a prior neighbor is not protection; it is the opposite. The friendly conversation in which the old owner said the fence was fine where it was converts the possession into permissive use. A claimant who offers that conversation as evidence of a settled boundary has handed the other side its defense.
Permission by a predecessor binds the successor's claim. The grant need not have come from the current owner. Permission extended to the claimant's predecessor in interest is enough.

For an owner on the other side of this, the corollary is that granting permission in writing is the mechanism the law provides for stopping a developing claim. What that document should say, and what it should avoid conceding, is not a form exercise.

sections.heading: What are the seven-year alternatives in chapter 7.28 RCW?

paras.p: Washington has shorter routes, with conditions much harder to meet.

Color of title plus taxes. A person in actual, open, and notorious possession under claim and color of title made in good faith, who continues in possession for seven successive years and during that time pays all taxes legally assessed on the land, is adjudged the legal owner to the extent of the paper title. RCW 7.28.070. Note the three added requirements: a written instrument that appears to convey title, actual good faith, and payment of every tax for every one of the seven years.

Vacant and unoccupied land. A person having color of title made in good faith to vacant and unoccupied land who pays all taxes assessed on it for seven successive years is deemed the legal owner to the extent of the paper title. RCW 7.28.080. The statute includes a trap: if anyone with a better paper title pays the taxes for even one year of the seven, the claimant loses the benefit of the section.

Title deducible of record. A seven-year period also applies to a possessor holding a connected title in law or equity deducible of record from the state or the United States, or from certain officers authorized to sell land for unpaid taxes or on execution. RCW 7.28.050.

The pattern is deliberate: where the claimant has a document and has paid the taxes, the legislature shortened the period and added a good faith requirement, which under the ordinary ten-year route is not an element at all. The paths are not interchangeable, and choosing wrong wastes a case.

sections.heading: Can I count the years my predecessor possessed the land?

paras.p: Sometimes you can, under a doctrine called tacking. Where there is privity between successive occupants holding continuously and adversely to the true title holder, the successive periods of occupation may be tacked to each other to compute the required 10-year period of adverse holding.

Privity is the whole fight. It is not enough that two people in sequence used the same strip; there must be a relationship connecting their possessions, ordinarily meaning something passed from one to the other. Whether a particular sequence of deeds, sales, and informal handovers creates that connection gets resolved on the documents and the testimony, not on the doctrine.

sections.heading: How is a prescriptive easement different?

paras.p: A prescriptive easement gives a right to use land. Adverse possession transfers ownership. The doctrines are analogous and Washington courts analyze them along similar lines, but the remedy differs and so do the elements.

To establish a prescriptive easement, the claimant must use another person's land for ten years and show that the use was open and notorious, that it was continuous or uninterrupted, that it occurred over a uniform route, that it was adverse to the landowner, and that it occurred with the knowledge of the owner at a time when the owner was able in law to assert and enforce his rights. The uniform route requirement has no counterpart in adverse possession, and it defeats claims built on wandering, occasional use.

Gamboa also settled a muddled question, and the answer favors landowners. The Washington Supreme Court held that an initial presumption of permissive use applies to enclosed or developed land cases in which there is a reasonable inference of neighborly sufferance or acquiescence, and it described what constitutes such a reasonable inference as a fairly low bar. The claimant bears the burden of proving the elements. A neighbor who has driven across a road the other owner built and maintained, without interfering with anything, starts from behind.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: Assuming maintenance equals ownership. Ten years of mowing a strip is not a legal conclusion. It is one fact bearing on whether the possession was the kind an owner would exercise over that land, and standing alone it usually is not.

Relying on the old neighbor's blessing. The most damaging error available, because the claimant volunteers the fact that kills the claim. Permission negates hostility, and a friendly understanding with a prior owner is permission.

Doing nothing while a claim matures. An owner who notices the encroachment and decides it is not worth a confrontation is letting a limitation period run. Ten years is not long in the life of a fence. And public land does not work this way at all: the color-of-title provisions do not reach land owned by the United States or this state, school lands, or lands held for any public purpose. RCW 7.28.090.

Believing that winning the argument settles the title. Possession does not clear the record. Making the boundary marketable requires an action to quiet title, brought by a person having a valid subsisting interest in real property and a right to possession, with judgment quieting title or removing a cloud. RCW 7.28.010. Until a court enters that judgment and it is recorded, the next title company to examine the parcel sees the recorded line, not the fence. So does a buyer's lender.

Overlooking the costs and tax provisions. In adverse possession actions filed on or after July 1, 2012, a prevailing claimant may be required to reimburse the record title holder for taxes paid during the claimant's possession and to pay unpaid taxes to the county treasurer, allocated as the court finds equitable. The court may also award costs and reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party where it determines an award is equitable and just. RCW 7.28.083. Winning is not free, and losing can be expensive.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here that you cannot do yourself

paras.p: The elements are public; the work is in the evidence and the procedure. That means establishing the ten-year window with sources that survive cross-examination, which often means aerial photography, tax records, utility records, prior surveys, and the recollections of people who lived there then. It means reading the chain of title for the privity tacking requires, and for the permission that defeats the claim. It means choosing between the ten-year route and a seven-year statutory route based on what the documents actually support. And it means bringing or defending a quiet title action, because a judgment is the only thing that makes the result marketable. These cases are tried on testimony about what happened on a strip of ground twenty years ago, and the side that assembled that record first usually prevails.

That is the work I do. title: Easements and Boundary Disputes in Washington: Scope Is the Real Fight
titleTag: Washington Easements and Boundary Disputes | Justin D. Leigh
description: How Washington easements are created, what yours actually permits, who maintains a shared road, and what happens when a fence or garage crosses the line.
lede: The gravel road to your house crosses the neighbor's field, and the neighbor has just put a gate across it. Or you hold a recorded easement and the neighbor is running a utility line under it. Or a surveyor staked your line last week and the result puts your garage two feet onto somebody else's property.
intro: Most easements and boundary disputes in Washington are not arguments about whether a right exists. The deed usually says it does. They are arguments about how far the right extends, who maintains it, and whether a court will order anyone to move anything.

sections.heading: What kinds of easements does Washington recognize?

paras.p: Express easements come from a written grant or reservation, and Washington requires the writing: every contract creating or evidencing an encumbrance upon real estate must be by deed. RCW 64.04.010.

Easements implied by prior use arise when land in common ownership is divided and an existing use continues. The claimant must prove unity of title in a common grantor, severance of that title, a prior apparent and continuous quasi-easement benefiting one part of the estate at the expense of another, and that the easement is reasonably necessary for proper enjoyment of the dominant estate. Unity of title and severance are absolute requirements, and no amount of necessity substitutes for them.

Easements by necessity come from the policy against leaving land landlocked and useless. A claimant need not show prior use but must prove strict necessity rather than reasonable necessity, which is a materially higher bar. Merely poor access does not qualify.

Prescriptive easements are earned by use. The claimant must use another's land for ten years and show the use was open and notorious, continuous or uninterrupted, over a uniform route, adverse to the owner, and with the owner's knowledge at a time when the owner could assert his rights. Implied and prescriptive easements are both disfavored, because each takes rights without a transaction, and the claimant carries the burden. I covered that route and how permission defeats it under adverse possession and prescriptive easements.

sections.heading: What does my easement actually let me do?

paras.p: Scope is where these cases are won. An express easement is construed like a contract, and the object is the intent of the original parties, taken from the deed as a whole. If the plain language is unambiguous, extrinsic evidence will not be considered. If ambiguity exists, extrinsic evidence is allowed to show the intentions of the original parties, the circumstances of the property when the easement was conveyed, and the practical interpretation given by the parties' prior conduct or admissions.

A utility case shows how narrowly that reads. The Court of Appeals held that the grant of a right of way for "road purposes" does not authorize the owner of the dominant estate to install utility lines under the road, finding no basis for defining road purposes beyond a way established for travel of persons, animals and vehicles. Two words in a 1955 contract decided whether a parcel could get power and water across its own access road.

The doctrine cuts both ways. Because the law assumes the parties contemplated natural development of the benefited property, subdividing that parcel has been held not to overburden an easement granted to serve it. Whether a change is natural development or overburdening is a fact question about intent, not a rule you can look up. Prescriptive easements are narrower still, because the extent of the right is fixed and determined by the user in which it originated. Ten years of driving a pickup across a field earns the right to drive a pickup across a field, not to widen the track for logging trucks.

sections.heading: Who has to maintain a shared access road?

paras.p: The default surprises most neighbors. The burden of maintaining an easement lies with the holder of that easement rather than the owner of the servient property. The owner whose land is crossed ordinarily owes nothing toward grading, graveling, plowing, or repair.

That default yields to a written agreement, which is why parcels sharing one road should have a recorded maintenance agreement allocating cost and setting a decision rule. Where no agreement exists and four owners share a deteriorating half-mile of gravel, the law supplies a rule about who owes a duty and almost nothing about how to divide a bill. That gap is why these disputes last years.

sections.heading: What does a survey settle, and what does it not?

paras.p: A survey is a licensed professional's opinion locating a written legal description on the ground, and only a land surveyor may sign, stamp, or seal a map or description filed as a public record. RCW 58.09.030. It is usually the most valuable document in a boundary dispute. It is not a judgment, and it does not move a line.

Two competent surveyors can reach different conclusions from the same deeds, because the deeds contain conflicts that rules of construction have to resolve. Where a description's courses and distances conflict with natural objects, the natural objects control, on the reasoning that errors in measurement are likelier than errors about an identifiable creek or rock. State ex rel. 609 (1915). Artificial monuments such as streets and railways likewise control over measured courses and distances. So a survey tells you where a surveyor believes the line is, and if the neighbor's surveyor disagrees, only a judgment fixes it.

sections.heading: What happens when a fence or garage crosses the line?

paras.p: Being right and getting a remedy are different questions, and here the gap is widest. Washington courts have held that an encroachment can render title unmarketable even where it measured only a few inches. 561 (1931). A two-foot garage encroachment is a title problem that surfaces at the worst moment, which is when the owner tries to sell or refinance.

Ordinarily a mandatory injunction will issue to compel removal. But a court may withhold it as oppressive, leaving damages as the remedy, where the encroacher did not simply take a calculated risk or act in bad faith, negligently, willfully or indifferently in locating the structure; the damage to the landowner was slight and the benefit of removal equally small; there was ample remaining room for a suitable structure and no real limitation on future use; it is impractical to move the structure as built; and there is an enormous disparity in resulting hardships.

The first factor does most of the work, and it is about the encroacher's state of mind when the structure went up. The benefit of balancing the equities is reserved for the innocent defendant who proceeds without knowledge or warning that his structure encroaches upon another's property or property rights. A letter putting a neighbor on notice before the concrete is poured changes the landscape permanently, and a neighbor who keeps building after notice has given up the defense.

sections.heading: What can I do about the neighbor's tree?

paras.p: Overhanging branches that interfere with your use of the property can be a nuisance. Washington defines an actionable nuisance to include an obstruction to the free use of property that essentially interferes with the comfortable enjoyment of life and property. RCW 7.48.010. An owner injuriously affected may sue and, on judgment, obtain a warrant directing the sheriff to abate the nuisance, or an injunction where abatement would be inadequate. RCW 7.48.020. The older case law recognizes a landowner's right to cut offending branches encroaching over the line. 298 (1921).

Now the part that generates lawsuits. Whoever cuts down, girdles, or otherwise injures or carries off any tree, timber, or shrub on the land of another without lawful authority is liable, and judgment for the plaintiff shall be for treble the amount of damages claimed or assessed. RCW 64.12.030. Mature trees are expensive, and trebled they become very expensive. A separate statute imposes treble damages plus investigative costs and reasonable attorney fees for wrongfully causing waste or injury to another's land, though it does not apply where liability is provided under the timber trespass statute. RCW 4.24.630.

The mitigating provision is narrower than defendants hope. If the trespass was casual or involuntary, or the defendant had probable cause to believe the land was his own, judgment shall be given only for single damages. RCW 64.12.040. Whether a contractor who cut to a line someone pointed at had probable cause is exactly what gets litigated. The distance between lawful trimming and a trebled judgment is a few feet and one question about who owns the trunk.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: Landlocked parcels sold without recorded access. A buyer purchases a back parcel relying on the road everyone has always used, and no recorded easement serves it. What remains is an implied easement or one by necessity, both disfavored and expensive. The related trap is a grantor purporting to grant more than he still owns. In Castanza the seller had already conveyed the servient parcel, and the court held that, being divested of ownership of the servient estate, the seller could not broaden the easement. A grant from someone who no longer owns the land conveys nothing.

Easements described by a feature that no longer exists. An easement over "the existing bulldozed road," or running "to the old barn," works until the road is regraded or the barn burns. Decades later the parties argue from aerial photographs. A description tied to a recorded survey survives; one tied to an object does not.

Assuming the title report settles it. An easement shown as an exception tells you a document exists. It does not tell you its width, route, permitted uses, or who maintains it, and the policy does not insure that you can use it as you intend. That is a separate read, which is why I wrote about how to read a preliminary title commitment.

Letting it escalate past the point where either side can afford to be right. Two neighbors litigating over a strip worth a few thousand dollars can each spend many times that, and fees are recoverable in some of these actions and not others.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here that you cannot do yourself

paras.p: The rules are findable. The difficulty is that nearly every question here resolves into a fact question about intent, answered from documents written by people who are long gone. That means reading the entire chain of title rather than the current deed, because the easement was usually created two or three owners back and its scope is fixed by what those parties meant. It means working with a surveyor to translate an old description into a line on the ground, and knowing which conflicts the rules of construction resolve and which they do not. It means evaluating encroachment claims against the Arnold factors honestly, including what your own side knew and when. And it means bringing or defending the actions that fix the problem, which are quiet title and ejectment under chapter 7.28 RCW, because only a judgment makes a boundary marketable. RCW 7.28.010.

That is the work I do. I am an independent attorney in downtown Spokane, and real estate is the largest part of my practice: easement and access disputes, boundary and encroachment matters, shared road disagreements, timber trespass claims, and quiet title and ejectment actions, in Spokane County Superior Court and the surrounding Inland Northwest counties. Easements and boundary agreements here are recorded with the Spokane County Auditor.

title: Do You Need a Will or a Trust in Washington?
titleTag: Will or Trust in Washington? | Justin D. Leigh
description: A Spokane attorney explains what a will does, when a revocable trust is actually worth it in Washington, and why beneficiary forms quietly override both.
lede: You have been meaning to deal with this for three years. Somebody at work mentioned a living trust, and now you are not sure whether the will you signed in 2011 is worth anything or whether you need something more elaborate. The choice between a will or a trust in Washington turns less on how much money you have than on what kind of property you own, where it sits, and who is named on the forms you filled out years ago and have not looked at since.

sections.heading: What a will does, and what it cannot reach

paras.p: A will says who receives your probate property, names the person who will administer your estate, and nominates a guardian for your minor children. Under RCW 11.12.010, any person of sound mind who has reached eighteen may dispose of an estate by will.

What a will cannot reach is property that passes by operation of law the instant you die. Your 401(k) goes to whoever is named on the plan's beneficiary form, a payable-on-death account goes to the named payee, and community property subject to a community property agreement vests in the surviving spouse with no court involvement at all. A will governs what is left over, which for many Washington households is a surprisingly small slice.

sections.heading: How a will has to be signed in Washington

paras.p: The rules for signing a will are less intuitive than people expect, and they are set out in RCW 11.12.020. The will must be in writing and signed by the testator, or by another person at the testator's direction and in the testator's presence. It must then be attested by two or more competent witnesses, who sign in the testator's presence and at the testator's direction.

Washington does not require the testator to sign in front of the witnesses, nor the witnesses to sign in front of each other. It does require that the witnesses sign within the testator's line of vision. A handwritten will with no witnesses is invalid if executed here, though Washington recognizes one validly executed under the law of the place of signing or of the testator's domicile.

The companion provision is RCW 11.20.020(2), which lets a witness sign a sworn affidavit reciting what the witness would otherwise testify to in court. That affidavit, written on the will or attached to it, is what makes a will self-proving, and its value is that it stops mattering whether your witnesses can be found decades later.

sections.heading: Is a revocable living trust worth it in Washington?

paras.p: Sometimes, and less often than the seminar circuit suggests. The usual pitch is probate avoidance, and that pitch was written for states where probate is slow and expensive. Washington is not one of them. The WSBA's estate planning deskbook puts it plainly: Washington's nonintervention probate procedure has simplified probate here so that living trusts are not as commonly used, and the expense of funding a trust is itself a reason they see less use in a state where probate costs are relatively low.

There are real reasons to use one. Real estate in another state would otherwise require a separate probate there. A beneficiary with a disability, a blended family, a closely held business, or a child whose inheritance needs managing rather than handing over all call for work a will cannot do. A trust also stays out of the public court file.

What a trust does not do is eliminate creditor exposure. If your assets sit in a revocable trust and nobody opens a probate, creditors have twenty-four months from your death to come forward. Chapter 11.42 RCW provides a notice-agent procedure that compresses that window, but somebody has to know it exists.

sections.heading: The community property agreement: Washington's quiet workhorse

paras.p: Washington is a community property state, and RCW 26.16.120 gives married couples a tool most states lack. A community property agreement can characterize property as community and provide for its status or disposition on the death of either spouse. In its common form it vests all community property in the survivor at the first death, with no probate.

The execution formalities are stricter than those for most estate planning documents. RCW 26.16.120 requires that provisions disposing of community property at death be in writing, signed by both spouses, and witnessed and acknowledged in the same manner as a deed to real estate. The statute also provides that the agreement "shall not derogate from the right of creditors," so it is not an asset protection device.

A second benefit has nothing to do with probate. Under I.R.C. § 1014(b)(6), both halves of community property take a new income tax basis when either spouse dies, not just the deceased spouse's half. For a couple holding appreciated real estate or securities, that feature alone is often worth more than everything else in the plan.

The hard limit is that the agreement reaches community property only. The Court of Appeals has invalidated provisions dividing a blended family's assets at the second death, because after the first death no community remains to operate on.

sections.heading: Your beneficiary designations are already overriding your will

paras.p: Washington's "super will" statute, RCW 11.11.020, lets a will redirect certain nonprobate assets, but only if the will specifically refers to the asset. A residuary clause does not do it. In one case a reference to "certain bank accounts and savings accounts" held in joint names was held not to include payable-on-death accounts. And under RCW 11.11.020(4), a will can only preempt a designation already in place when the will was signed. Change the form afterward and the form wins.

sections.heading: Powers of attorney and health care directives

paras.p: The documents that matter while you are alive get the least attention. Washington's Uniform Power of Attorney Act, Chapter 11.125 RCW, requires that a power of attorney be signed and dated, and either notarized or attested by two or more competent witnesses who are not the principal's caregivers. RCW 11.125.050(1).

Two traps live in that chapter. A power of attorney is durable, meaning it survives your incapacity, only if the document says so. RCW 11.125.040. One that is not expressly durable terminates at the moment it becomes necessary. And authority over health care is not swept in by a general grant of broad authority; RCW 11.125.240(1)(l) requires express authorization. The separate health care directive comes from Washington's Natural Death Act, Chapter 70.122 RCW, which addresses life-sustaining treatment in a terminal or permanent unconscious condition and carries its own restrictive witness rules. RCW 70.122.030(1).

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: Four failures account for most of the damage.

The trust nobody funded. A revocable trust controls only assets actually titled in its name. People sign a beautiful trust instrument, never transfer the house or the brokerage account, and die with an empty trust and a pour-over will. Washington validates those pour-over gifts under RCW 11.12.250, so the plan does not fail outright. It just produces the probate the trust was bought to avoid.

The ex-spouse on the retirement account. RCW 11.07.010 revokes a nonprobate beneficiary designation in favor of a former spouse when a marriage ends, and many people assume that solves it. It frequently does not, because the United States Supreme Court has held that ERISA preempts that statute where the asset belongs to an ERISA-governed plan. Your employer's 401(k) and group life insurance are those plans, and the administrator pays whoever is on the form.

The online will that was never properly witnessed. The document is usually fine; the execution is what fails. In In re Estate of Ricketts, the witnesses signed only the self-proving affidavit and not the codicil, and the court held that did not satisfy RCW 11.12.020. The statute was later amended to let a witness sign either the will or a conforming affidavit, but the testator's signature still has to appear on the will itself. These mistakes surface when the signer is gone.
Assuming the will controls everything. The gap between what people think their will governs and what it actually governs is where litigation is born.

sections.heading: Does Washington have its own estate tax?

paras.p: Yes, and it is separate from the federal one. Washington enacted a standalone estate tax in 2005, codified at Chapter 83.100 RCW, which has operated independently of federal changes since. The Washington exclusion amount is lower than the federal exemption, so families who owe nothing federally can still owe Washington tax. Portability does not apply here either, meaning a surviving spouse does not inherit the deceased spouse's unused Washington exclusion the way the federal system allows. The exclusion figure is adjusted over time and has been amended by the Legislature, so the current number is worth confirming rather than assuming. A return is due within nine months of death. RCW 83.100.050(2).

sections.heading: Planning for minor children

paras.p: You can nominate a guardian for your children in your will, and you should, though a court still has to appoint. The harder question is who manages the money and on what terms, because a child who inherits outright receives everything at eighteen, in one piece.

sections.heading: Why this is lawyer work

paras.p: The drafting is not the hard part. The hard part is inventory and coordination. Before a document gets written, somebody has to establish how every asset is titled, what every beneficiary form says, whether a community property agreement from a previous decade is still operative, and whether separate property has been commingled without anyone intending it. Those answers determine which documents you need, and reversing the order is how people end up with an elegant plan governing a fraction of what they own.

sections.heading: About my practice

paras.p: I am an independent attorney in downtown Spokane, and estate planning is the largest part of my practice. I prepare wills, revocable and irrevocable trusts, community property agreements, powers of attorney, and health care directives, and I handle the probates and estate disputes that follow when planning was not done or did not hold. I am admitted in Washington and in Oregon, which matters for Inland Northwest families holding property on both sides of the Columbia. Spokane County estates are administered in Spokane County Superior Court, where I appear regularly.

paras.p: If you are not sure whether your current documents still do what you think they do, that is a short conversation and worth having. I offer a free initial consultation by appointment at my office in downtown Spokane.

title: Probate in Washington: What Actually Happens After a Parent Dies
titleTag: Probate in Washington State | Justin D. Leigh
description: A Spokane attorney walks through Washington probate: when it is required, how nonintervention powers work, and the creditor deadline that exposes executors.
lede: Your mother died eleven days ago. There is a will somewhere, a house with a mortgage, a bank that will not talk to you, and a sibling who has opinions. Somebody told you probate takes years and eats a third of the estate, which is true in some states and is not true here. Probate in Washington is one of the more efficient systems in the country, and understanding why will tell you a great deal about the next several months.

sections.heading: Is probate required in Washington?

paras.p: Often it is not. No Washington statute compels you to open a probate. Whether you need one depends on what the decedent owned and how it was titled.

If everything passed outside probate, by community property agreement, beneficiary designation, payable-on-death account, survivorship, or a funded trust, there may be nothing for a probate to administer. If there is real property titled in the decedent's name alone, you will almost certainly need one, because no bank, buyer, or title company will accept a conveyance from someone with no authority to sign.

One obligation does not depend on opening a probate. RCW 11.20.010 requires the person holding the will to either deliver it to the named personal representative or file it with the court within thirty days of learning of the death, and a named personal representative has forty days to file it. Willful failure can create liability to anyone damaged by the delay. The will gets filed even when no probate follows.

sections.heading: The small estate affidavit

paras.p: For modest estates there is an alternative to probate entirely. Under RCW 11.62.010, where the assets otherwise subject to probate are valued at less than $100,000 and include no interest in real property, a successor can claim the decedent's personal property by affidavit rather than through an estate administration.

Three limits define it. Only personal property transfers this way, so a single parcel of real estate takes the procedure off the table. Only a "successor" as defined in RCW 11.62.005(2) may use it, meaning a beneficiary under the will or by intestacy, or a surviving spouse or domestic partner as to their half of the community property; creditors cannot. And advance written notice to the other successors is required.

The bank that transfers in reliance on a valid affidavit is released from liability. The recipient is not. Under RCW 11.62.020 the claiming successor remains accountable to any personal representative later appointed.

sections.heading: Opening the estate and admitting the will

paras.p: A probate is opened by petition in the superior court of the county where the decedent lived. In Spokane County that is Spokane County Superior Court. The court admits the will, appoints a personal representative, and issues letters testamentary, which is the document the bank will finally accept.

One misconception is worth correcting early: the eldest child is not automatically in charge. If there is a will, the person named in it has first claim to serve. If there is no will, RCW 11.28.120 sets the priority, running surviving spouse or registered domestic partner first, then children, then father or mother, then brothers or sisters, then grandchildren, then nephews or nieces. Birth order does not appear in the statute, and in every case the authority comes from a court appointment rather than family consensus.

sections.heading: Nonintervention powers, and why Washington probate is efficient

paras.p: This is the feature that distinguishes Washington, and the reason the horror stories you have read do not describe what is about to happen to you.

A personal representative may petition for "nonintervention powers" under Chapter 11.68 RCW. RCW 11.68.011 sets two threshold conditions: the will must not specifically preclude them, and the estate must be solvent. If those are met, the court may grant the powers where the petitioner is the personal representative named in the will, or, in an intestate estate, where the petitioner is the surviving spouse or domestic partner, the estate consists solely of community property, and all of the decedent's reasonably identifiable living issue are also that spouse's issue. A petitioner outside those categories can still seek the powers after notice under RCW 11.68.041.

What the powers do is remove the court from the administration. Under RCW 11.68.090 a personal representative holding them may borrow money for the estate, lease or mortgage or encumber estate property, sell or exchange it, make interim distributions, and settle the estate, all without notice to the court and without a court order. The Supreme Court has put the consequence directly, holding that the superior court has no role in administering a nonintervention estate except in narrow, statutorily enumerated situations.

In a supervised probate every significant act requires a hearing. In a nonintervention probate, after appointment the personal representative administers much as a trustee would, and most estates never see a courtroom again.

sections.heading: Creditor claims, and the deadline that matters most

paras.p: Notice to creditors is optional in Washington. The personal representative is not required to publish it. Publishing is usually the right call anyway, because it starts a short clock instead of a long one.
How long a creditor has depends entirely on what the personal representative did, and the four possibilities are set out in RCW 11.40.051:

Where notice was published and a reasonably ascertainable creditor received actual notice, the claim is barred on the later of thirty days from service or mailing of that notice or four months after first publication. RCW 11.40.051(1)(a).
Where notice was published and the creditor was not reasonably ascertainable, the claim is barred four months after first publication. RCW 11.40.051(1)(b)(i).
Where the creditor was reasonably ascertainable but received no actual notice, the claim is not barred until twenty-four months after the date of death. RCW 11.40.051(1)(b)(ii).
Where no notice was published at all, claims are barred twenty-four months after the date of death. RCW 11.40.051(1)(c).

Two refinements change how those periods actually operate. The claims statute shortens the time to come after an estate, but it does not extend any otherwise applicable statute of limitations. RCW 11.40.051(2). And claims satisfiable entirely from liability or casualty insurance proceeds sit outside these deadlines under RCW 11.40.060, which is why a car accident claim can surface long after you thought the estate was closed.

sections.heading: Inventory, accounting, distribution, and closing

paras.p: The personal representative prepares an inventory and appraisement of estate assets as of the date of death under RCW 11.44.015. In a nonintervention estate it is not automatically filed, but any beneficiary, any unpaid creditor who has filed a claim, or the Department of Revenue may request a copy, and it must be furnished within ten days. RCW 11.44.015(2). Under RCW 11.44.035 a party in interest may challenge the inventory at any stage.

Closing is usually done by a declaration of completion under RCW 11.68.110 rather than by petitioning for a decree of distribution. A copy goes to each party who has not waived notice, with the statutory notice of filing. Those parties then have thirty days to ask the court to review the reasonableness of fees or to request an accounting. If nobody does, the personal representative's actions and fees are deemed approved and discharge is automatic.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: Distributing before the creditor period runs. This is the serious one. A personal representative who pays the beneficiaries early and then faces a valid claim has no estate left to pay it from and is looking at personal exposure. The related trap runs the other way: because notice to creditors is optional, a fiduciary who skips notice and thereby forces payment of a claim that publication would have barred can be personally liable for the difference. Both failures come from treating the creditor machinery as paperwork rather than as the thing that protects the person administering the estate.

Missing the nonclaim deadline from the creditor's side. If you are owed money by someone who died, the four-month window after first publication is short, strictly applied, and nobody is obligated to remind you.

Real property never conveyed out. This is among the most common problems in the practice area. A parent dies, the family divides things informally, nobody probates anything, and title to the house still stands in the name of someone who has been dead for decades. It stays invisible until somebody tries to sell or refinance, at which point it is a title defect that has to be cured under time pressure, with heirs who may be scattered or deceased themselves.

Treating the role as honorary. A personal representative is a fiduciary. Under RCW 11.28.250 a court may remove one for waste, embezzlement, mismanagement, fraud, incompetence, wrongful neglect, or any other necessary cause. RCW 11.68.070 extends removal or restriction to a nonintervention personal representative who fails to execute the trust faithfully, and lets a prevailing beneficiary recover attorney fees. The Supreme Court has confirmed the catch-all ground reaches a nonintervention personal representative too.

sections.heading: Why this is lawyer work

paras.p: Most of a probate is judgment, not forms. Whether to petition for nonintervention powers, whether to publish notice to creditors and when, whether a particular asset is even part of the estate, whether a claim should be paid or rejected, how to handle a beneficiary who wants a distribution now against a creditor period with four weeks left. Those decisions carry personal consequences for the person serving, and they are made in sequence, where an early choice closes off later options. A probate also puts one family member in a fiduciary role over property siblings believe is partly theirs, at the worst possible moment emotionally, and having the deadlines calendared and the correspondence handled from outside the family prevents a meaningful number of the disputes that otherwise arrive six months in.

sections.heading: About my practice

paras.p: I handle probate and estate administration from my office in downtown Spokane, and it is a substantial share of my practice. I represent personal representatives through nonintervention and supervised administrations, advise successors on whether a small estate affidavit will do the job, prepare and respond to creditor claims, clear title to real property never conveyed out of a prior estate, and litigate estate disputes when they arise. Spokane County probates proceed in Spokane County Superior Court, and I appear in the surrounding Inland Northwest counties as well.

paras.p: If someone close to you has died and you are not sure whether a probate is necessary or who is supposed to be doing what, that is worth sorting out before decisions get made that are hard to undo. I offer a free initial consultation by appointment in downtown Spokane.

title: Will Contests, Trustee Disputes, and TEDRA in Washington
titleTag: TEDRA Estate Disputes in Washington | Justin D. Leigh
description: A Spokane attorney explains TEDRA, the four-month will contest deadline, undue influence, and how Washington routes estate disputes into mediation first.
lede: Your father signed a new will fourteen months before he died. It leaves most of what he had to the person who was driving him to appointments, and it was drafted by a lawyer nobody in the family had heard of. You are not sure whether what you are feeling is grief or a legal claim. In Washington the answer runs through a statute most people have never heard of and a deadline shorter than almost anyone expects.

sections.heading: What TEDRA is, and why Washington is different

paras.p: The Trust and Estate Dispute Resolution Act, Chapter 11.96A RCW, is Washington's unified framework for resolving disagreements about estates, trusts, powers of attorney, and nonprobate assets. It is unusual in two respects.

The first is breadth. TEDRA defines a "matter" expansively and gives the superior court authority over essentially any dispute arising under Title 11 RCW, so one procedure handles a will construction question, a trustee accounting demand, and a removal petition alike. An action is commenced by filing a petition under RCW 11.96A.100, which differs from ordinary civil practice where service can start the case.

The second is that TEDRA pushes disputes toward resolution rather than trial. It contains its own mediation and arbitration track, and it gives the court a broad fee-shifting power. Under RCW 11.96A.150 a court may award costs and attorney fees to any party, from any other party or from the assets of the estate or trust, as it determines to be equitable. That provision reaches all of Title 11 and is not limited by the narrower fee statutes elsewhere in it; the Supreme Court has applied it in a will contest. The effect is that both sides carry risk from the first filing, which disciplines marginal claims and stonewalling fiduciaries alike.

sections.heading: The deadline, which is the first thing to find out

paras.p: A will contest must be brought within four months of the order admitting the will to probate, or rejecting it. RCW 11.24.010. If no contest is filed in that window, the probate or rejection is binding and final.

The cases are unforgiving. The four months is not extended by CR 6(e) even where interested parties received notice of the will's admission by mail. The contest is commenced by filing, not service, and the contestant must then personally serve the personal representative within ninety days of filing; failure means the action is deemed never commenced for limitations purposes. The courts have also rejected electronic mail as sufficient service. Untimely service has been treated as a total failure to comply rather than substantial compliance.
The clock therefore starts when the will is admitted, not when you find out about it, and not when you learn the facts that make you suspicious.

sections.heading: Who can contest

paras.p: Standing is a threshold question, not a formality. Under RCW 11.24.010 "any person interested" may contest, which the courts have defined as a person with a direct, immediate, and legally ascertainable interest in the devolution of the estate, one that would be impaired by probate of the will or benefited by a declaration that it is invalid. The interest must be a present pecuniary one with the characteristics of a property right. Intestate heirs qualify, as do beneficiaries under a prior will who would receive less under the will being challenged. Moral claims, however genuine, do not.

sections.heading: The grounds, and the one that actually gets litigated

paras.p: A will can be challenged for lack of testamentary capacity, undue influence, improper execution, or fraud. They are not equally useful.

Capacity is difficult because the presumption runs the other way. Where a will is rational on its face and executed with the required formalities, the law presumes the testator had capacity. The standard is also lower than people assume, requiring an understanding of the transaction, a comprehension of the nature and extent of the property, and a recollection of the natural objects of the testator's bounty. A dementia diagnosis is not the same thing as incapacity on the day of signing.
Improper execution is mechanical. It either happened correctly or it did not.

Undue influence is where these cases live, because it is provable circumstantially and because it describes what actually happens. The governing authority sets out what courts since have called the signposts of undue influence. The three most important are that the beneficiary occupied a fiduciary or confidential relationship with the testator, that the beneficiary actively participated in preparing or procuring the will, and that the beneficiary received an unusually or unnaturally large part of the estate. Added to those are the testator's age and condition of health and mental vigor, the nature and degree of the relationship, the opportunity to exert influence, and the naturalness of the will itself.

The procedural consequence is what makes this ground powerful. A sufficient combination of a confidential relationship and suspicious circumstances can raise a presumption of undue influence and shift the burden to the beneficiary to prove the will was not procured by it, and shifting that burden frequently decides the case. Where the influence affected only part of the instrument, RCW 11.24.010 and.040 allow a will to be partially invalidated rather than thrown out entirely.

sections.heading: Fiduciary disputes: accountings and removal

paras.p: Many estate disputes are not about the document but about the person administering it.

Trustees have a statutory duty to account. Under Chapter 11.106 RCW a trustee appointed by will, deed, or agreement must give permissible distributees annual statements of receipts and disbursements, and any party may petition for an accounting under RCW 11.96A.080. The duty of loyalty is codified at RCW 11.98.078, which the Court of Appeals has applied to personal representatives holding nonintervention powers.

Removal of a personal representative is available under RCW 11.28.250 for waste, embezzlement, mismanagement, fraud, incompetence, wrongful neglect, or any other necessary cause. Where the personal representative holds nonintervention powers, RCW 11.68.070 supplies the route, and a prevailing petitioner may recover attorney fees. On the trust side, an action against the trustee of an express trust for breach of fiduciary duty must be brought within three years of the earliest of discovery or reasonable discovery of the breach, the trustee's discharge, or termination of the trust.

sections.heading: The mediation and arbitration track

paras.p: This part of TEDRA has no close analog, and it is why a Washington estate dispute does not have to become a trial.

Under RCW 11.96A.300 any party may cause a matter to be subject to mediation by serving a statutory notice of mediation. A party who does not want to mediate must affirmatively object within a short statutory window, and the notice and objection procedures are exacting enough that the Court of Appeals has found a notice non-compliant.

If mediation fails, arbitration is available under RCW 11.96A.310 on a parallel structure. An arbitration decision can be appealed by requesting a trial de novo within thirty days of its filing, and there the fee consequence hardens: RCW 11.96A.310(10) makes an award of costs and attorney fees to the prevailing party mandatory, taking precedence over the court's general discretion.

Alongside this, RCW 11.96A.220 lets the parties resolve a matter by written nonjudicial agreement carrying the same effect as a court order, including modifying or terminating a trust, provided all parties consent. Where a party is a minor, incapacitated without a guardian of the estate, unborn, unascertained, or cannot be located, a special representative may be appointed to bind that party. RCW 11.96A.250.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: Waiting. This is the one that ends cases before they start. Families spend the four months after the will is admitted gathering documents, talking to relatives, and deciding whether they really want to do this. By the time the decision is made the right to contest is gone, and no amount of evidence revives it. The contest statute has no tolling for disability and no equitable exception.

Litigating a small estate into nothing. Fee-shifting under RCW 11.96A.150 cuts both ways, and legal fees are indifferent to the size of the estate. A dispute over a few tens of thousands of dollars can consume a meaningful fraction of it while the parties establish who was right. Deciding early and honestly what the realistic recovery is, measured against cost, is part of the representation.

"He promised me the house." Oral promises to leave property are not hopeless in Washington, but they are hard. A claimant must prove the decedent agreed to leave the property, that the services contemplated as consideration were actually rendered, and that they were rendered in reliance on the contract. The evidentiary bar is high: the contract must be established by evidence that is conclusive, definite, and beyond all legitimate controversy. Years of caretaking with nothing in writing is the most common version, and the claims that succeed tend to involve substantial, documented care.

sections.heading: Why this is lawyer work

paras.p: The first task in an estate dispute is not building the argument. It is figuring out what the clock says: which deadline governs, when it started, and whether the thing you intend to file is a will contest under Chapter 11.24 RCW, a fiduciary action, a creditor claim, or a contract claim, because each carries different limitation periods and standards. Getting that wrong is usually fatal and rarely fixable. After that the work is evaluative. Whether a given set of facts raises the undue influence presumption and shifts the burden is a judgment experience informs, as is whether a dispute belongs in mediation, in arbitration, or in front of a judge.

paras.p: I handle trust and estate disputes from my office in downtown Spokane, alongside the estate planning and probate work that produces most of them. I represent beneficiaries challenging wills and trusts, fiduciaries defending their administration, and parties on both sides of accounting and removal petitions. I appear in Spokane County Superior Court and the surrounding Inland Northwest counties, and I use TEDRA's mediation and nonjudicial agreement procedures where they can resolve a matter without the cost of trial.
