title: Forming a Washington LLC, and the Operating Agreement That Actually Governs It
titleTag: Washington LLC Operating Agreement | Justin D. Leigh
description: A Washington LLC operating agreement that says nothing still has rules: chapter 25.15 RCW supplies them, and the defaults rarely match what the owners agreed.
lede: Two people go into business together. One has money, the other has the trade and the customer list, and they agree to split things fairly. The LLC gets filed online in twenty minutes, nobody writes down what "fairly" means, and eighteen months later they are arguing about who can sign a lease and how much each of them gets paid. Without a Washington LLC operating agreement, chapter 25.15 RCW resolves that argument, and rarely the way either person expected.

sections.heading: Choosing an entity is two questions, not one

paras.p: The first question is liability. In a Washington LLC the debts and liabilities of the company are solely the company's, and no member or manager is personally obligated for them solely by reason of being a member or manager. RCW 25.15.126(1). The shield has limits people miss, because a member remains personally liable for their own torts and can always agree by contract to be personally obligated, which is exactly what a landlord or a bank will ask for. RCW 25.15.126(2), (3). A sole proprietorship offers no shield at all, and in a general partnership all partners are jointly and severally liable for all obligations of the partnership. RCW 25.05.125(1). A corporation under Title 23B RCW offers a shield with a more rigid governance structure built in.

The second question is tax, and chapter 25.15 RCW does not answer it. Federal tax classification and Washington's business and occupation tax are separate bodies of law, which is why "LLC or S corporation" is two questions wearing one coat: the S corporation is a tax election rather than a kind of entity. Decide liability and tax separately, then confirm the two answers are compatible.

sections.heading: What forming a Washington LLC actually involves

paras.p: Formation is the easy part. One or more persons execute a certificate of formation and deliver it to the Secretary of State, stating the company's name, its registered agent's name and address, the address of its principal office, a dissolution date if there is to be one, and the name and address of each signer. RCW 25.15.071(1). The company exists when the Secretary of State files it, as a separate legal entity with perpetual existence unless the certificate says otherwise. RCW 25.15.071(2), (3).

The obligations that keep it alive are the ones that get dropped. A Washington LLC must continuously maintain a registered agent in this state, file an initial report within one hundred twenty days, and file an annual report after that. RCW 25.15.021(1); RCW 25.15.106; RCW 23.95.255(1), (2). Fail to do it and the entity is administratively dissolved. RCW 23.95.255(7). State business licensing under chapter 19.02 RCW, city licensing, and any trade-specific license are separate tracks. None of this creates the deal between the owners, because formation creates the entity and the operating agreement creates the business relationship.

sections.heading: What chapter 25.15 RCW does when your agreement is silent

paras.p: The Washington limited liability company act, RCW 25.15.904, contains one provision worth reading twice. The limited liability company agreement governs relations among the members and the rights and duties of a manager, and "to the extent the limited liability company agreement does not otherwise provide for a matter described in subsection (1) of this section, this chapter governs the matter." RCW 25.15.018(1), (2).

There is accordingly no such thing as an LLC with no governance rules. There are only LLCs governed by a Washington LLC operating agreement the owners negotiated and LLCs governed by statutory defaults the owners never read. Several of those defaults surprise people.

Voting is per capita, not by money in. Member action requires the affirmative vote of a majority of the members, so the member who contributed two hundred thousand dollars and the member who contributed two thousand have one vote each, unless the agreement sets voting on a profit share, class, or other basis. RCW 25.15.121(1), (4).
Amending the agreement takes unanimity. Amending it requires the consent of all members, and so does admitting a new one. RCW 25.15.121(2)(b), (d), (e).

Distributions follow contribution value, not headcount. Absent an agreement, distributions are made in proportion to the agreed value of the contributions each member made and is required to make. RCW 25.15.206. Two people who think of themselves as equal partners can have unequal distribution rights, and the fight will be about what "agreed value" was.

There is no right to money along the way. A member has no right to any distribution before dissolution and winding up unless the company decides to make an interim one. RCW 25.15.211. Anyone counting on undocumented quarterly draws is counting on goodwill.

In a member-managed company, every member can bind it. Each member is an agent with authority to bind the company in the ordinary course of its activities, and the manager-managed alternative has to be chosen. RCW 25.15.151(2); RCW 25.15.154.

Interests are transferable, and the transferee gets money without a voice. A transfer carries the distributions the transferor would have received, but not management participation or member information rights. RCW 25.15.251(1), (2). An ex-spouse, a creditor, or an heir can end up holding an economic stake in a company whose decisions they have no part in.

Services can be capital. A contribution may consist of money, property, services performed, promissory notes, or contracts for future services, which is why the agreed value of sweat equity has to be written down at the time. RCW 25.15.191.

A short list of matters cannot be contracted around at all, RCW 25.15.018(3), and the one that matters most in a dispute is that no agreement may vary a court's power to order dissolution under RCW 25.15.274.

sections.heading: What a Washington LLC operating agreement should resolve

paras.p: The agreement is a list of decisions the owners would rather make now, while they agree, than later. Those decisions include who manages and what size of commitment requires everyone's sign-off; what each member contributes, in what form, at what agreed value; whether and when distributions are made, including distributions sized to cover each member's tax on income allocated to them; what restricts a transfer, and what happens to an interest on death, divorce, bankruptcy, or departure; how a deadlock gets broken; and how someone exits, which means a valuation method and payment terms rather than a statement that the company may buy the interest. Each turns on the business, the bargaining positions, and the tax posture, which is why a form cannot answer them.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: Founders who never papered the split. Two people who agreed on sixty-forty and never wrote it down are equal voters by default, with distribution rights keyed to the agreed value of their contributions, and no document establishing either figure. RCW 25.15.121(1); RCW 25.15.206. The dispute becomes a credibility contest about conversations from three years ago.

An internet form that contradicts the real deal. Downloaded agreements are usually drafted for another state, and the law of this state governs a Washington LLC's internal affairs regardless. RCW 25.15.033. The deeper problem is that an executed agreement is the deal. If the form says distributions are pro rata to units and the members actually agreed one of them takes a management draw first, the form wins.

Commingling. Members are personally liable to the extent that shareholders of a Washington business corporation would be in analogous circumstances, and a court may consider the established veil-piercing case law in deciding it. RCW 25.15.061. The statute forgives one formality, in that failing to hold meetings is not a factor where the certificate and agreement do not require them. It forgives nothing about running company money through a personal account.

The fifty-fifty company with no way out. Equal votes, no buy-sell, no deadlock mechanism, and a disagreement neither member will concede. The default remedy is litigation, because on application by a member or manager the superior court may order dissolution where it is not reasonably practicable to carry on the company's activities in conformity with the certificate and the agreement, or where other circumstances render dissolution equitable. RCW 25.15.274. Avoiding that lawsuit is most of what a Washington LLC operating agreement is for.

sections.heading: Why this is lawyer work

paras.p: Drafting is not the hard part. The hard part is getting the deal out of the founders, because most of what matters has never been discussed: what happens when one of them wants to work twenty hours a week, what happens when the business needs capital only one of them has, what happens when one of them dies. The job is to ask those questions while everyone is still friendly, then make the agreement, the certificate, the nonwaivable provisions of RCW 25.15.018(3), and the tax structure consistent with one another. Provisions that read cleanly in a Word document also behave differently when a party is actively trying to defeat them.

title: Land Use Permits and Appeals in Washington: Why the Deadline Decides Most Cases
titleTag: Washington Land Use Permit Appeal | Justin D. Leigh
description: A Washington land use permit appeal is barred unless it is filed and served inside a very short statutory window. What that window is, and when it starts.
lede: A notice appears on a pole at the edge of the lot behind your house, describing something you have to read three times to understand. Or you are on the other side of it, a year and real money into a project at a county planning department, and a neighbor has just filed something. The first question a lawyer asks is not whether the decision was right. It is what date it issued, because a Washington land use permit appeal runs on a clock measured in days, and once that clock expires the merits stop mattering.

sections.heading: Who actually writes the rules that govern your property

paras.p: Washington land use regulation is local, with a statutory frame around it. Under the Growth Management Act, chapter 36.70A RCW, planning counties and cities adopt a comprehensive plan with mandatory elements that include land use, housing, capital facilities, utilities, and transportation, and they must then act in conformity with that plan. RCW 36.70A.070; RCW 36.70A.120.

The plan is policy about how areas are intended to develop over twenty years, while the zoning code and the development regulations are the enforceable rules a planner applies to an application, so a parcel whose plan designation contemplates multifamily housing is not thereby zoned for it. That distinction also decides the forum. A challenge to a plan or a development regulation itself goes to the Growth Management Hearings Board within sixty days after publication, RCW 36.70A.290(2), while a challenge to a particular permit decision goes to superior court.

sections.heading: How a project permit gets processed

paras.p: Chapter 36.70B RCW governs local project review. Within twenty-eight calendar days of receiving an application, the local government must tell the applicant in writing whether it is procedurally complete, and the statute says expressly that this determination is not a substantive review and is not conditioned on the adequacy, accuracy, or sufficiency of what was submitted. RCW 36.70B.070(1), (2). A notice of application follows within fourteen days, stating a comment period of not less than fourteen and not more than thirty days, and a project needing permits in more than one category gets a single open record hearing and no more than one closed record appeal. RCW 36.70B.110(2); RCW 36.70B.120(2). That is the whole window in which an ordinary member of the public participates, and it closes before most people have formed a view about the project.

sections.heading: Who decides a conditional use, a variance, or a rezone?

paras.p: It depends on the local code, and the statute explaining why is worth knowing. A code city may adopt a hearing examiner system and vest in the examiner authority over conditional uses, variances, subdivisions, shoreline permits, administrative appeals, and SEPA appeals, and counties have parallel authority. RCW 35A.63.170(1); RCW 36.70.970.

Here is the part that catches people. The city's ordinance must specify the legal effect of the examiner's decisions, and the statute offers three choices: a recommendation to the legislative body, an administrative decision appealable to the legislative body, or, except for a rezone, the final decision of the legislative body. RCW 35A.63.170(2). The same kind of application can be a recommendation in one city and a final decision in the next one over, so whether a further local appeal exists is answered by reading that jurisdiction's code. Rezones add a wrinkle, because a site-specific rezone is quasi-judicial while area-wide rezones and annexations are legislative approvals the judicial review statute excludes from the definition of a land use decision. RCW 36.70C.020(2)(a).

sections.heading: SEPA review and what a threshold determination really is

paras.p: The State Environmental Policy Act, chapter 43.21C RCW, overlays all of this. A threshold determination is required for any proposal that meets the definition of an action and is not categorically exempt, the lead agency's responsible official makes it, and it is documented as either a determination of nonsignificance or a determination of significance. WAC 197-11-310(1), (2), (5). It is due no later than ninety days after the application is complete. RCW 43.21C.033(1).

The substance is narrower than people assume. The responsible official reviews the environmental checklist, decides whether the proposal is likely to have a probable significant adverse environmental impact, and considers mitigation the agency or the applicant will implement as part of the proposal. WAC 197-11-330(1). A determination of nonsignificance is therefore not a finding that a project has no environmental effects. It is a determination that the effects, with mitigation folded in, do not rise to probable significant adverse impacts. Neighbors read a DNS as a whitewash and applicants read it as a clearance, and both overstate it.

sections.heading: The appeal deadline: the Land Use Petition Act

paras.p: A Washington land use permit appeal that reaches court does so under chapter 36.70C RCW, which may be cited as the land use petition act and is the exclusive means of judicial review of land use decisions, subject to listed exceptions. RCW 36.70C.005; RCW 36.70C.030(1). Three features of it decide most cases before anyone argues about zoning.

What counts as the decision. A land use decision is a final determination by the local jurisdiction's body or officer with the highest level of authority to make it, including those with authority to hear appeals. RCW 36.70C.020(2). If the local code provides an appeal to a hearing examiner, the planner's letter is generally not the land use decision and the examiner's ruling generally is. Where a timely motion for reconsideration is filed, the land use decision occurs when the decision on reconsideration is entered.

The clock, and that it governs service too. A land use petition "is barred, and the court may not grant review," unless it is both timely filed with the court and timely served on the parties the statute lists, which include the local jurisdiction, each applicant and property owner named in the written decision, and each person named in the decision who appealed to a local quasi-judicial decision maker. RCW 36.70C.040(2). The petition is timely if filed and served on all of them within twenty-one days of the issuance of the land use decision. RCW 36.70C.040(3). Issuance has its own definition, three days after a written decision is mailed, or if it is not mailed, the date the jurisdiction gives notice that the decision is publicly available. RCW 36.70C.040(4)(a).

That structure is what hurts people. The deadline is short, it is unforgiving, it requires completed service rather than merely filing, and it runs from a statutory issuance date instead of the day you found out. I am giving the figure from the current statutory text, and you should still confirm both the deadline and its starting point against the statute as it reads today and against the specific local code, because the code determines which decision in the chain is final, and that determines when the clock started.

What the court can do. Review is not a second hearing. The superior court sits without a jury, reviews the record, and may grant relief only if the petitioner establishes one of six standards, running from unlawful procedure and erroneous interpretation of law to a lack of substantial evidence. RCW 36.70C.130(1). Standing is limited, and a person who is not the applicant or owner must show that the decision prejudices them, that their interests were among those the jurisdiction had to consider, and that they have exhausted their administrative remedies to the extent required by law. RCW 36.70C.060(2).

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: The neighbor who learns about the project too late. Participation happens during the comment period in the notice of application, under notice methods that include posting the property, newspaper publication, and mailing to neighboring owners. RCW 36.70B.110(2), (4). Someone who misses all of it faces two problems rather than one, because the twenty-one-day clock may already be running and the exhaustion requirement may bar them even inside it. RCW 36.70C.060(2)(d).

The applicant who builds during an appeal. A stay is available but never automatic, and a court may grant one only on findings that the requesting party is likely to prevail, will suffer irreparable harm without it, that a stay will not substantially harm other parties, and that the request is timely. RCW 36.70C.100(2). Without a stay, construction proceeds at the owner's risk.
Failure to exhaust. Where the local code provides an administrative appeal, it is a prerequisite rather than an option, and skipping it ends the case without a ruling on anything.

Vesting assumptions that do not hold. A valid and fully complete building permit application is considered under the ordinances in effect on the date of application, and the same holds for preliminary plats and short plats. RCW 19.27.095(1); RCW 58.17.033(1). Two qualifications undercut the confident version of that rule. What counts as fully complete is defined by local ordinance, which is not the same thing as procedural completeness under RCW 36.70B.070, and vesting does not restrict conditions imposed under SEPA. RCW 19.27.095(2), (6); RCW 58.17.033(3).

sections.heading: Why this is lawyer work

paras.p: Most of the work in a Washington land use permit appeal happens before any argument about the merits. Someone has to read the local code to identify which decision is the final land use decision, assemble and serve the correct party list under RCW 36.70C.040(2), decide whether the real target is the project decision, the regulation, or a SEPA determination, and get the administrative record before the court. Getting any one of those wrong forecloses the rest. On the applicant side the job runs in reverse, building a record during the local process that can survive review.

paras.p: I am an independent attorney in downtown Spokane, at 601 W. 1st Ave., Suite 1400, admitted in Washington and in Oregon. Land use, zoning, and permitting is a regular part of my practice, alongside real estate transactions and litigation, business and regulatory work, and civil litigation, and these matters run through county and city planning departments, hearing examiners, and superior courts across eastern Washington.

paras.p: If you have received a land use decision, or just learned that one issued, the date on it is the first thing to look at, and a Washington land use permit appeal is not something to start late. My office offers a free initial consultation by appointment in downtown Spokane.

title: Washington Liquor Licenses and LCB Compliance: The Rules That Catch Owners Off Guard
titleTag: Washington Liquor License & LCB Rules | Justin D. Leigh
practiceArea: Alcohol Beverage Licensing and Regulatory Compliance
description: A Washington liquor license stays with the applicant, not the business, and the tied-house rules reach deals that look like ordinary marketing. What to watch.
lede: You have a purchase and sale agreement for a neighborhood bar, a closing date, and a price allocation with a line item for the liquor license. Or you run a brewery, and a restaurant has offered to build a dedicated tap wall if you help pay for the sign. Both are ordinary commercial instincts, and both run into the regulatory architecture around alcohol here. A Washington liquor license is not an asset that travels with a business, and the rules about who may give what to whom reach conduct that looks like nothing more than marketing.

sections.heading: Who regulates alcohol in Washington, and under what law

paras.p: Title 66 RCW is the state's alcohol statute, built on the 1933 act that may be cited as the Washington State Liquor Act. RCW 66.98.010. It is administered by a three-member board known as the Washington state liquor and cannabis board, with broad rulemaking authority. RCW 66.08.012; RCW 66.08.030. The Board's rules are Title 314 WAC, and they hold most of the operational detail, so an owner who reads only the statute misses half the regime.

License categories turn on what a business does with alcohol rather than what it calls itself. On-premises retail includes the spirits, beer, and wine restaurant license and the beer and wine restaurant license, while off-premises retail includes the grocery store license and the beer and wine specialty shop license. RCW 66.24.400; RCW 66.24.320; RCW 66.24.360; RCW 66.24.371. Producers have their own tiers, with separate licenses for microbreweries, domestic wineries, distilleries, and craft distilleries, each carrying tasting-room conditions written into the statute. RCW 66.24.244; RCW 66.24.170; RCW 66.24.140; RCW 66.24.145. A business has the privileges its license grants and nothing broader, so a taproom that begins hosting ticketed dinners may have outrun its license.

sections.heading: The three-tier system is more subtle than people expect

paras.p: Most people understand the three-tier system as a flat prohibition, with producers, distributors, and retailers kept separate and nobody owning across the lines. In Washington that is no longer accurate. The Legislature found that the historical total prohibition on holding an interest in one tier while holding an interest in another "is unduly restrictive." RCW 66.28.280.

What replaced it is a standard rather than a bar. It is lawful for an industry member to hold a direct or indirect financial interest in a retailer, and for a retailer to hold an interest in an industry member, unless the interest has resulted or is more likely than not to result in undue influence or in an adverse impact on public health and safety. RCW 66.28.290(1), (2). That is better news for business planning and worse news for certainty, because the test is qualitative and somebody else applies it.

Two rules keep the standard from collapsing. First, except for promotional items specifically allowed by RCW 66.28.310, no industry member may advance and no retailer may receive money or money's worth "under an agreement written or unwritten or by means of any other business practice or arrangement." RCW 66.28.305. That language reaches informal arrangements, and it is what turns a brewery paying for a bar's sign into a problem. Second, the Board decides, because any person may request a Board determination on a financial interest, and if the Board finds undue influence it may issue an administrative violation notice or a notice of intent to deny a license, and where the transaction has already closed it may require that the transaction be rescinded or otherwise undone. RCW 66.28.300.

The advertising rules work the same way, barring a retail licensee's name from a manufacturer's, importer's, or distributor's advertising and permitting a brand name in a retailer's own advertising only where nothing of value was exchanged for the mention. WAC 314-52-090.

sections.heading: Applying: the local authority notice and the objection window

paras.p: Every license issues in the name of the applicant, and the holder may not allow anyone else to use it. RCW 66.24.010(1). The Board may inspect the premises, inquire into all matters connected with its construction and operation, and consider prior criminal conduct and violation history. RCW 66.24.010(2). A sole proprietor applicant must have lived in Washington at least a month, and a corporation or LLC must be formed here or hold a certificate of authority. RCW 66.24.010(1)(a), (d). No applicant may exercise any privilege until the Board approves the application. WAC 314-07-015(3).

Applicants underestimate the objection track. The city or town, or the county legislative authority, may file written objections with the Board against the applicant or the premises within twenty days after the notice of application is transmitted. RCW 66.24.010(8)(c). The Board must also notify churches, schools, and designated public institutions within five hundred feet, and it may not license previously unlicensed premises within five hundred feet of a tax-supported public elementary or secondary school, measured between entrances, if the school objects in writing within twenty days. RCW 66.24.010(9)(a). A lease signed before anyone measured that distance is a lease on space that may not be licensable.

sections.heading: The licensed premises is a boundary, not an address

paras.p: The Board's rules define licensed premises as all areas under the licensee's legal control that are available to or used by customers or employees in the conduct of business operations, and they add that specific alcohol consumption areas must be approved by the Board, which makes the approved floor plan part of the license. WAC 314-01-005(1).

Changes to that footprint require approval from the licensing division. Any alteration affecting the size of the customer service area requires approval, the licensee submits two sets of floor plans, and service in the altered area may begin only after the local liquor enforcement officer inspects it. WAC 314-03-300(1). Excluding patrons under twenty-one, reclassifying a lounge for an event, extending service outdoors, and sharing a service area with a non-licensee each have their own rule. WAC 314-03-300(2) through (4); WAC 314-03-200; WAC 314-03-215. Licensed premises are also open to inspection, and refusing to allow it is itself a violation. RCW 66.28.090.

sections.heading: A license does not come with the business

paras.p: This is the most expensive misunderstanding in the field. Because a Washington liquor license issues in the name of the applicant, it does not convey by a bill of sale, and prior Board approval is required before an ownership change. WAC 314-07-080(1). A change in the qualifying persons of a sole proprietorship or a partnership requires a new application at the annual fee, while a change in a corporation's officers or stockholders, or in an LLC's members or managers, requires the corresponding application. WAC 314-07-080(1). Stock and unit transfers are tracked cumulatively against a ten percent threshold, so a series of small transfers can trigger an obligation no single transfer would, and who counts as an owner is governed by the true party of interest rules. WAC 314-07-080(3); WAC 314-07-035.

Temporary retail licenses exist, and they are what buyers reach for when they assume a license can be handed over at closing, but a temporary license is a discretionary Board action with its own grounds for denial and revocation. WAC 314-07-055; WAC 314-07-060. The closing date and the licensing timeline are two different schedules, and an agreement that treats them as one has allocated a risk nobody priced.

sections.heading: When an administrative violation notice arrives

paras.p: Enforcement runs on a short clock. After the Board notifies a licensee of an alleged violation, the licensee has twenty days from receipt to do one of three things on the agency's form: accept the recommended penalty, request a settlement conference in writing, or request an administrative hearing in writing. WAC 314-29-005; WAC 314-29-010(1). Doing nothing is itself a choice with a consequence, because absent a response within twenty days the recommended suspension takes effect. WAC 314-29-010(2)(a).

A settlement conference is a real process. The licensee and a hearing examiner or enforcement captain discuss the circumstances, the recommended penalty, and any aggravating or mitigating factors, and a compromise the Board approves becomes part of the licensing history. WAC 314-29-010(3). That matters more than it looks, because penalties escalate with violation history. WAC 314-29-015. Formal action is an adjudicative proceeding under chapter 34.05 RCW, with one exception to a prior hearing: the Board may summarily suspend a license for up to one hundred eighty days on a finding that public health, safety, or welfare imperatively require emergency action. RCW 66.08.150(4).

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: Buying a bar and assuming the license comes with it. Prior Board approval of the ownership change is required, and the new owner may not exercise any privilege until approval issues. WAC 314-07-080; WAC 314-07-015(3).

A tasting-room or event arrangement that crosses a tier. The money's worth prohibition and the advertising rules both reach the co-branded release party, the subsidized sign, and the offer to help with tap handles, and the Board can require a closed transaction to be undone. RCW 66.28.305; WAC 314-52-090; RCW 66.28.300.

Altering the premises first and asking later. Expanding a patio or adding a service bar changes the customer service area and requires approval, plans, and inspection before service begins. WAC 314-03-300(1).
Treating a violation notice as a parking ticket. The twenty-day window closes, the suspension attaches, and the history follows the license into the next matter.

sections.heading: Why this is lawyer work

paras.p: The hard part is not reading any single rule. It is that the answer to a business question usually lives in three places at once, with a prohibition stated in Title 66 RCW, an exception defined in Title 314 WAC, and an agency practice about structure that neither document describes. Deal timing is the other recurring problem, because purchase agreements and financing commitments get signed on commercial schedules while licensing runs on its own.

title: Section 1983 Claims in Washington: Civil Rights Lawsuits Against Government
titleTag: Section 1983 Claims in Washington | Justin D. Leigh
description: What a section 1983 claim in Washington requires, how qualified immunity works, when a city is liable, and the filing deadlines that quietly end these cases.
lede: An officer put you on the ground during a traffic stop and you still cannot lift your arm over your head. A city council voted on a permit in a meeting nobody was told about. You asked a sheriff's office for body camera footage four months ago and have heard nothing. Those are three different problems with three different sets of rules. Only the first is the territory of a section 1983 claim in Washington, and the other two run on state statutes most people have never heard of.

sections.heading: What does 42 U.S.C. § 1983 actually require?

paras.p: Section 1983 is not a list of rights. It is the vehicle for suing over rights that come from somewhere else, usually the Constitution. The statute reaches "[e]very person who, under color of any statute, ordinance, regulation, custom, or usage, of any State" subjects another person "to the deprivation of any rights, privileges, or immunities secured by the Constitution and laws."

Each phrase there is a place a case can fail. The defendant must be a "person" the statute reaches, and must have acted "under color" of state law rather than as a private individual. The right at stake must be a federal right, which means a government employee's decision that was unfair, mistaken, or even cruel is not automatically a constitutional violation. A section 1983 claim in Washington turns on whether the conduct maps onto a specific federal right, not on whether it was wrong.

sections.heading: Which constitutional violations come up most often?

paras.p: Excessive force and unlawful seizure under the Fourth Amendment. Force used in an arrest or stop is analyzed under the Fourth Amendment's "objective reasonableness" standard, weighing "the severity of the crime at issue, whether the suspect poses an immediate threat to the safety of the officers or others, and whether he is actively resisting arrest or attempting to evade arrest by flight," judged "from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene, rather than with the 20/20 vision of hindsight." Id. at 396. Under that framing the officer's actual intent drops out, and so does negligence in the lead-up.

First Amendment retaliation. This requires protected speech or conduct, an adverse action, and a causal link, with the adverse action measured by "whether an official's acts would chill or silence a person of ordinary firmness from future First Amendment activities."

Due process. Procedural claims turn on whether a protected liberty or property interest existed and what process was owed before the government took it. Substantive claims are harder, because the conduct must "shock the conscience" rather than merely be negligent.

sections.heading: What is qualified immunity, and why does it stop so many cases?

paras.p: This is the central obstacle, and nobody should learn about it from the other side's brief. Qualified immunity shields officials performing discretionary functions "from liability for civil damages insofar as their conduct does not violate clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known."

The phrase doing the work is "clearly established," and saying the Constitution forbids excessive force is not enough. "[F]or a constitutional right to be clearly established, its contours 'must be sufficiently clear that a reasonable official would understand that what he is doing violates that right.'" Hope does set a limit, rejecting any requirement that earlier cases be "materially similar" and holding that "officials can still be on notice that their conduct violates established law even in novel factual circumstances." Id. at 741. Even with that breathing room, the defense ends a great many claims, and it can end them without the court ever deciding whether what happened was unconstitutional, which is why precedent research belongs before a complaint is drafted.

sections.heading: Can you sue the city itself?

paras.p: Not simply because its employee violated your rights. The rule is that "a local government may not be sued under § 1983 for an injury inflicted solely by its employees or agents," and that the entity answers only "when execution of a government's policy or custom... inflicts the injury."

That means proving a formal policy, a practice so persistent it functions as policy, a decision by a final policymaker, a failure to train, or ratification after the fact. None is established by the incident alone, and the proof usually sits in records the agency holds. One counterweight is worth knowing: qualified immunity belongs to the individual official, and municipalities "have no immunity from damages liability flowing from their constitutional violations."

sections.heading: Federal or state court, and how long do you have?

paras.p: Either court can hear a section 1983 claim in Washington, and state court often appeals to plaintiffs because Washington tort claims against government officers carry no qualified immunity defense. Section 1983 itself has no limitation period, so federal courts borrow the forum state's general personal injury period, which in Washington is the three-year period in RCW 4.16.080(2) covering "any other injury to the person or rights of another not hereinafter enumerated." The trap is that companion state claims can expire sooner, since assault, battery, and false imprisonment carry two years under RCW 4.16.100(1).

State tort claims against government also require a presentment step that federal claims do not. A claim against a city, county, or district goes to the entity's appointed claim agent on the standard tort claim form, and no suit may be filed until sixty calendar days pass, with the limitation period tolled meanwhile. RCW 4.96.020. Claims against the State go to the Office of Risk Management, with the same sixty-day wait. RCW 4.92.100; RCW 4.92.110. Those presentment statutes do not apply to the section 1983 claim itself.

sections.heading: Washington's Public Records Act: what a records request actually does

paras.p: Chapter 42.56 RCW gives Washington residents a disclosure right most states do not match. It opens with the declaration that "[t]he people of this state do not yield their sovereignty to the agencies that serve them," and it directs that the chapter "be liberally construed and its exemptions narrowly construed." RCW 42.56.030.

Any person may request identifiable records from a state or local agency without giving a reason, and the agency then has five business days to respond in one of a handful of permitted ways: produce the records, point to them online, give a reasonable time estimate, seek clarification, or deny the request. RCW 42.56.520. Silence is not on that list, and silence is itself a violation.

Enforcement is what gives the Act teeth. A requester may bring a show-cause action in superior court, where review is de novo and the burden sits on the agency. A prevailing requester is awarded costs and reasonable attorney fees, and the court may add up to one hundred dollars for each day a record was unlawfully withheld. RCW 42.56.550. The action must be filed within one year of the agency's claim of exemption or its last installment production. RCW 42.56.550(6).

sections.heading: The Open Public Meetings Act: how a public body must meet

paras.p: Chapter 42.30 RCW requires that "[a]ll meetings of the governing body of a public agency shall be open and public." RCW 42.30.030(1). The reach of that sentence surprises people, because "action" is defined to include "receipt of public testimony, deliberations, discussions, considerations, reviews, evaluations, and final actions." RCW 42.30.020(3). Deliberating behind closed doors is the problem, not just voting there.

The consequences are concrete. An ordinance, resolution, or directive adopted outside a properly noticed open meeting is "null and void," as is any vote taken by secret ballot. RCW 42.30.060. Members who knowingly attend such a meeting face a personal civil penalty, and a person who prevails against the agency is awarded costs and reasonable attorney fees. RCW 42.30.120. Executive sessions are allowed only for the purposes the statute enumerates, and that list is narrower than many agencies assume. RCW 42.30.110.

sections.heading: Where these claims go wrong

paras.p: The deadline runs while the client waits. People spend a year on internal complaints, then arrive with a two-year assault claim that expired months ago.
A required pre-suit claim form was never presented. The omission surfaces after filing and often cannot be cured in the time left.
The conduct was unfair but not unconstitutional. An arbitrary supervisor, a code officer who was wrong, a hearing that felt rigged—none is a federal claim without an identified federal right.

A records request is written as a question. Asking how many complaints an agency received is a request for information, which the agency may decline. Asking for records referring to those complaints triggers the disclosure duty.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here that you cannot do alone

paras.p: Most of the value sits in work done before anything is filed: identifying the precise federal right, searching the case law for decisions specific enough to put a reasonable official on notice, choosing the theory against the entity, and running each claim's deadline separately. Someone also has to say plainly when the obstacles are high, because a clear-eyed read early is worth more than optimism.

I am admitted in Washington, WSBA #55307, and Oregon, OSB #242384.

title: Washington's Law Against Discrimination: What It Covers That Federal Law Does Not
titleTag: Washington Law Against Discrimination | Justin D. Leigh
description: How Washington's WLAD reaches further than Title VII, what a harassment or retaliation claim requires, and why filing windows differ by claim and by forum.
lede: You were told your position was eliminated three weeks after you asked about medical leave. Or a supervisor has been making comments for most of a year, you reported it, and now your schedule has changed in ways nobody will explain. The most useful thing a Washington worker can learn is that state law reaches further than the federal law most people have heard of, and covers people and employers Title VII does not reach.

sections.heading: What the Washington Law Against Discrimination covers

paras.p: The Washington Law Against Discrimination, chapter 49.60 RCW, is usually called the WLAD, and two of its sections do most of the work in an employment case. RCW 49.60.030(1) declares a civil right to be free from discrimination because of "race, creed, color, national origin, citizenship or immigration status, sex, honorably discharged veteran or military status, sexual orientation, or the presence of any sensory, mental, or physical disability or the use of a trained dog guide or service animal by a person with a disability," and it includes within that right "[t]he right to obtain and hold employment without discrimination." Subsection (2) gives an injured person a civil action for an injunction, actual damages, or both, "together with the cost of suit including reasonable attorneys' fees."

RCW 49.60.180 then lists what an employer may not do, and its list of protected characteristics is not identical. It adds age and marital status, which do not appear in RCW 49.60.030(1). That difference decides which statutory hook a worker's claim hangs on and, sometimes, whether the worker is covered at all.

sections.heading: Where WLAD is broader than federal law

paras.p: The employer size threshold is lower. The WLAD defines an "employer" as a person "who employs eight or more persons." RCW 49.60.040(11). Title VII applies to employers with fifteen or more employees. Someone at a ten-person Spokane company has a state claim and no federal one.

Sexual orientation is in the statute by name. It means "heterosexuality, homosexuality, bisexuality, and gender expression or identity," and expressly covers having or being perceived as having a gender identity different from the sex assigned at birth. RCW 49.60.040(29).

The definition of disability is wider. A WLAD disability is an impairment that is medically cognizable or diagnosable, exists as a record or history, or is perceived to exist whether or not it exists in fact, and it exists "whether it is temporary or permanent, common or uncommon, mitigated or unmitigated." RCW 49.60.040(7)(a)-(b).

Race is defined to include hair. Race "is inclusive of traits historically associated or perceived to be associated with race including, but not limited to, hair texture and protective hairstyles." RCW 49.60.040(21).

sections.heading: Do you have to file with the EEOC first?

paras.p: A federal Title VII claim ordinarily requires an administrative charge before any lawsuit. The charge goes to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and because Washington has a state civil rights agency with a work-sharing arrangement, filing with one generally counts as filing with the other.

Under 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5(e)(1) the baseline is 180 days after the alleged unlawful employment practice occurred. A 300-day period applies instead where the worker has initially instituted proceedings with a state or local agency with authority over the practice, which in Washington means the Human Rights Commission, and even on that longer track the charge comes due 30 days after notice that the state agency has terminated its proceedings if that date arrives first. A short further period then runs, after the right-to-sue notice issues, for filing the suit.

A claim under the Washington Law Against Discrimination works differently, because there is no administrative exhaustion requirement for a WLAD claim brought in court. A worker may instead complain to the Washington State Human Rights Commission, and RCW 49.60.230(2) then requires that complaint within six months of the alleged act, with one year for pregnancy discrimination and two years for whistleblower retaliation. In superior court the ordinary limitation period is three years, drawn from RCW 4.16.080(2), and for a discrete act such as a termination it starts on the date of the act.

These windows are short, and they differ by claim and by forum. One set of facts can produce a federal charge deadline measured in months and a court deadline measured in years, and missing the shortest closes that route.

sections.heading: What a hostile work environment claim actually requires

paras.p: Under Washington law the claim has four elements: language or conduct because of a protected characteristic, that was unwelcome, that affected the terms or conditions of employment, and that is imputed to the employer.

The third and fourth elements are where these cases are fought. Merely offensive conduct does not satisfy the third; it has to have been sufficiently severe or sufficiently pervasive, which are two separate routes, and one incident can be enough if it is extreme. On imputation, conduct is attributed to the employer directly where an owner, manager, or corporate officer personally participates, but where a supervisor or coworker created the environment the employee must show the employer authorized, knew, or should have known of the harassment and failed to take reasonably prompt and adequate corrective action. Glasgow, 103 Wn.2d at 407.

sections.heading: Retaliation and the duty to accommodate

paras.p: Retaliation is a distinct claim, not an aggravating detail. RCW 49.60.210(1) makes it an unfair practice to "discharge, expel, or otherwise discriminate against any person because he or she has opposed any practices forbidden by this chapter, or because he or she has filed a charge, testified, or assisted in any proceeding under this chapter." It can survive even where the underlying complaint was not itself a violation.

Accommodation runs on its own track. For accommodation purposes specifically, RCW 49.60.040(7)(d) requires that the impairment be known or shown through an interactive process to exist in fact, and then either that it substantially limit the person’s ability to do the job, or that the employer was put on notice and medical documentation shows a reasonable likelihood that working without accommodation would aggravate the impairment to that degree. A limitation "is not substantial if it has only a trivial effect." RCW 49.60.040(7)(e). The statute itself uses the phrase "interactive process," which tells you that what was said between employee and employer, and in what order, carries real weight.

sections.heading: Wrongful discharge in violation of public policy

paras.p: Washington also recognizes a common-law tort outside the WLAD. Four core situations have long been recognized: discharge for refusing to commit an illegal act, discharge for performing a public duty such as jury service, discharge for exercising a legal right such as filing a workers' compensation claim, and discharge in retaliation for reporting employer misconduct. A claim inside those four is not run through the four-factor framework reserved for novel public-policy claims. The tort also reaches past the WLAD's eight-employee floor, since the Supreme Court has applied it to private employers with fewer than eight employees.

sections.heading: Independent contractors, and why Washington differs from Oregon

paras.p: Most antidiscrimination law protects employees and stops there. The Washington Law Against Discrimination does not, and the controlling case is from Spokane. A golf professional under contract to operate one of the City's courses alleged sex discrimination in the negotiation and performance of that contract. The Washington Supreme Court held: "Applying general rules of statutory construction, we hold the broad recognition of rights contained in RCW 49.60.030(1) includes the right of an independent contractor to be free of discrimination based on sex, race, national origin, religion, or disability in the making or performing of a contract for personal services." Id. at 112-13.

The limits of that holding are part of what makes it useful. It rests on the general civil right in RCW 49.60.030(1), not the employer-unfair-practices section, and the Court was explicit that an independent contractor does not have the protection of RCW 49.60.180. The bases listed are also narrower than the list that applies to employees.

Oregon’s chapter, ORS 659A, by contrast covers only employees, and independent contractors do not enjoy its protections. Oregon is broader in a different respect, reaching a private employer with even one employee where Washington requires eight.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: Resigning before getting advice. A resignation changes the question from whether you were fired unlawfully to whether conditions were intolerable enough to count as a discharge, which is harder to show. People quit Friday and call Monday, and Monday is too late.
Missing an administrative window. Internal HR complaints, union grievances, and appeals to a supervisor stop no clock.

Assuming at-will employment means the employer may do anything. At-will means no good reason is needed, not that the employer may act for a prohibited reason, and it has no application to retaliation or the public-policy tort.

Assuming any unfair treatment is discrimination. A manager hostile to everyone, a demotion that really was about performance, favoritism toward a friend—none is unlawful without a link to a protected characteristic or protected activity.
Never gathering the evidence. Schedules, reviews, and the email where you reported it are where a claim is found or lost, and people lose account access the day they are walked out.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here that you cannot do alone

paras.p: Most of the work is characterization and sequencing. One fact pattern can support a WLAD disparate treatment claim, a hostile work environment claim, a retaliation claim, an accommodation claim, and a public-policy tort, each with its own elements, proof, and deadline, and some available in state court while others require an administrative charge first. Choosing which to bring, in which forum, and in what order is a decision made once and lived with.

title: Fathers’ Rights and Parenting Plans in Washington: What the Statute Actually Asks
titleTag: Fathers' Rights & Parenting Plans WA | Justin D. Leigh
description: What Washington's parenting plan statutes actually weigh, why parentage comes first for unmarried fathers, and where fathers' cases go wrong. Spokane lawyer.
lede: You have been served, or you are about to file, and the question underneath every other question is whether a Washington court is going to treat you as the backup parent. Search for fathers’ rights in Washington state and you will mostly find grievance rather than law. The statute Washington judges actually apply is written down, it is gender-neutral on its face, and knowing what it weighs changes how you approach your own case.

sections.heading: Washington does not use the word “custody”

paras.p: Washington replaced custody and visitation with a single governing document called a parenting plan. Under RCW 26.09.184, a permanent parenting plan must contain a residential schedule saying where each child lives on given days of the year, an allocation of decision-making authority over education, health care, and religious upbringing, and a process for resolving future disputes short of returning to court. Those three pieces move independently, so a parent can have fewer overnights and still hold joint decision-making, and people sign plans whose schedule looks tolerable without noticing what the decision-making paragraph did.

sections.heading: Does Washington law favor mothers?

paras.p: Nothing in chapter 26.09 RCW assigns a preference to either parent based on gender. RCW 26.09.002 makes the best interests of the child the standard and says that “the relationship between the child and each parent should be fostered unless inconsistent with the child’s best interests.”

Even so, the real asymmetry comes from the list of factors rather than from any preference in the text. RCW 26.09.187(3)(a) gives the court seven factors for the residential schedule and then adds one sentence that does more work than anything else in the chapter: “Factor (i) shall be given the greatest weight.” Factor (i) is the relative strength, nature, and stability of the child’s relationship with each parent, and factor (iii) asks whether a parent “has taken greater responsibility for performing parenting functions relating to the daily needs of the child.” Those functions, defined at RCW 26.09.004(2), are mundane on purpose: feeding, clothing, supervision, health care, day care, education. A father who did those things and can show it is arguing inside the statute, while a father arguing about how unfair the other parent has been is arguing about something the statute never asks.

sections.heading: When the court must limit a parent’s time

paras.p: Washington has a dedicated restrictions statute, and the Legislature substantially rewrote it in 2025. RCW 26.09.191 separates conduct that requires the court to limit a parent’s residential time from conduct that may lead to limits. The mandatory category includes willful abandonment, physical abuse or a pattern of emotional abuse of a child, a history of acts of domestic violence as defined in RCW 7.105.010, an assault causing grievous bodily harm or the fear of it, and any sexual assault, with sexual abuse of a child now handled under RCW 26.09.192. The discretionary category reaches more ordinary cases, including substantial nonperformance of parenting functions, long-term impairment from substance abuse, abusive use of conflict, and withholding a child from the other parent for a protracted period without good cause.

sections.heading: If you were never married to the mother, parentage comes first

paras.p: This is the most consequential point on this page and the one I see missed most often. A court cannot enter a residential schedule for a father whose parentage has not been established, and being on the birth certificate, paying for things, living with the child, and being universally known as the dad are not the same thing as a legal parent-child relationship. RCW 26.26A.100 lists how that relationship arises, including a statutory presumption, a signed acknowledgment, an adjudication, and adoption.

The presumptions at RCW 26.26A.115 mostly run through marriage or a state registered domestic partnership, which is why unmarried fathers fall outside them. One does not: a person who “resided in the same household with the child for the first four years of the life of the child” and “openly held out the child as the individual’s child” is presumed to be a parent. Short of that, an unmarried father relies on an acknowledgment of parentage under RCW 26.26A.200 or an adjudication under RCW 26.26A.400.

What follows from that is the part that hurts. A father who never established parentage has no order to enforce when the other parent decides he is not seeing the child this weekend, so parentage is the foundation and everything else waits on it.

sections.heading: The temporary order shapes the case more than people expect

paras.p: The statute tells the court to disregard the temporary plan when it writes the permanent one. RCW 26.09.191(2)(a) says the court “shall not draw any presumptions from the provisions of the temporary parenting plan.” That rule is real, and it is not the same as saying the temporary schedule does not matter, because RCW 26.09.002 also provides that a child’s best interest is ordinarily served when the existing pattern of interaction between parent and child is altered only as far as the changed relationship of the parents requires, and a temporary schedule that runs a year becomes that existing pattern.

Correspondingly, the motion setting that schedule is governed by RCW 26.09.194, and the required declaration tells you exactly what the court cares about: where the child has lived for the preceding twelve months, each parent’s performance during those twelve months of the parenting functions relating to the child’s daily needs, and both parents’ work and child-care schedules. Fathers who have that record rarely realize it, and fathers who do not rarely start building it until the hearing is a week out.

sections.heading: Child support is a separate calculation, and more time does not automatically lower it

paras.p: The economic table at RCW 26.19.020 sets a presumptive monthly obligation by combined monthly net income and number of children, and RCW 26.19.035 requires worksheets on the official statewide form, signed under penalty of perjury. RCW 26.19.075(1)(d) does let the court deviate downward when the child spends a significant amount of time with the paying parent, but the deviation is discretionary, and the court may not grant it if doing so would leave insufficient funds in the receiving household to meet the child’s basic needs. Trading residential time for a lower support number is a strategy that frequently produces neither.

sections.heading: After a plan is entered, changing it is harder

paras.p: Changing a parenting plan is a different proceeding with a deliberately high threshold. RCW 26.09.260 requires facts that arose since the prior plan or were unknown to the court, a substantial change in circumstances, and a modification necessary to serve the child’s best interests. RCW 26.09.270 then directs the court to deny the motion unless adequate cause for a hearing is established by the affidavits, and many petitions die there on the papers without anyone reaching the merits.

Separately, moving with a child runs on its own statute. Under the Child Relocation Act at RCW 26.09.405 through 26.09.560, RCW 26.09.440 requires sixty days’ advance notice in the ordinary case and a warning that the move will be permitted unless an objection is filed and served within thirty days. Most people also have the standard backward, because RCW 26.09.520 creates a rebuttable presumption that the relocation will be permitted and puts the burden on the objecting parent to show that the detrimental effect outweighs the benefit, across eleven unweighted factors.

sections.heading: Where fathers’ cases go wrong

paras.p: Self-help instead of a motion. A father who believes something is wrong at the other house, and responds by keeping the child or departing from the schedule, has created the clearest fact in the case, and it is a fact about him. Withholding a child for a protracted period without good cause is listed in RCW 26.09.191 as a basis for restricting residential time, and RCW 26.09.260 makes two contempt findings in three years a route to modifying the plan against him. The merits of the original concern do not rescue the method, because the remedy is a motion heard by the court and never a decision made in a driveway.
Agreeing to a temporary plan to keep the peace. A parent who accepts less temporarily, meaning to fix it at trial, ends up explaining at trial why the arrangement he agreed to should change.
Never establishing parentage. Years of being the father in every practical sense, and no order, until the first conflict exposes it.
Informal arrangements never entered as an order. Two cooperative parents work out a schedule and never put it in a plan, and it holds until one of them moves, remarries, or hires a lawyer.
Text messages and social media. Everything you write becomes an exhibit, and a parent’s own messages are often where the proof of abusive use of conflict comes from.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here that the forms cannot

paras.p: The Administrative Office of the Courts publishes mandatory pattern forms for all of this, free and public, and the forms are the easy part. Filling one in feels like completing a task, and it will accept almost anything you write on it. What the form does not do is tell you which of the seven residential factors your facts actually reach, how to compress twelve months of daily parenting into a declaration a commissioner reads in four minutes, or whether your facts support a restriction or expose you to one. Practice is local too, since Spokane County Superior Court has its own family law calendar, its own commissioners, and its own expectations about what a motion looks like.

sections.heading: About my practice

paras.p: I am Justin D. Leigh, an independent attorney in downtown Spokane. In family law I handle parenting plans, parentage, child support, modifications, relocation objections, and the restriction findings under RCW 26.09.191 that often decide the rest of the case, and I appear in Spokane County Superior Court and the surrounding Eastern Washington counties. I am admitted in Washington (WSBA #55307) and Oregon (OSB #242384), which matters here, because a parenting plan with a household on each side of the Columbia raises questions about which state decides and enforces.

sections.heading: If you want to talk about your own situation

paras.p: I offer a free initial consultation by appointment at my downtown Spokane office. If you are holding a petition, a relocation notice, or a parenting plan someone wants you to sign, bring the paperwork and a calendar of the last year.

title: Can My Lawyer Use AI? What It Does, What It Cannot Do, and What to Ask
titleTag: Can My Lawyer Use AI? What to Ask | Justin D. Leigh
description: A Washington lawyer explains what AI actually does in legal work, why fabricated case citations happen, how confidentiality is handled, and what to ask.
lede: You read that a lawyer somewhere got in trouble for filing a brief citing cases that did not exist, and now you are wondering whether the person handling your matter is doing the same thing. The short answer is that a lawyer can use AI, and the question that matters is how carefully, because most people have no way to evaluate that from the outside. I use AI in my practice every day, which means I can tell you where it genuinely helps, where it fails in a specific and predictable way, and what you are entitled to ask any lawyer you are thinking of hiring.

sections.heading: What AI is actually good at in legal work

paras.p: The useful applications are unglamorous and mostly about volume. A software system can read ten thousand pages of medical records or a decade of emails in minutes and tell you where a particular date, name, or phrase appears, which is work that used to consume weeks and still missed things. It can produce a first draft of a document whose structure is already known, summarize a long deposition well enough to tell you which forty pages you need to read, and organize a discovery production into something searchable. It can also check a sixty-page agreement for internal contradictions, defined terms used before they are defined, and cross-references pointing at the wrong section, which is exactly the sort of error a tired human reader skates past.

What all of those have in common is that the output is checkable. Somebody can look at the original and confirm the answer, which is the only condition under which this technology belongs anywhere near a legal matter.

sections.heading: What AI cannot do

paras.p: Two failures here are categorical rather than incidental, and the first one is the reason this page exists. A language model does not know whether a case exists. It produces text that resembles the text it was trained on, and a citation that looks exactly like a real citation is, from the model’s point of view, a success. It has no mechanism for distinguishing a real one from a plausible invention.

Beyond that, a language model does not exercise judgment. Deciding which of four arguments to lead with, which weakness to disclose and which to leave alone, whether a given judge will react badly to a particular tone, whether a client should settle at a number that is objectively low but subjectively right for their life, none of that is a text-generation problem. Strategy is the lawyer’s work. So is accountability, because a filing carries a signature, and no software can be the person who stands up and answers for it.

sections.heading: The fabricated citation problem, named plainly

paras.p: This is the failure that has produced actual discipline, and it is worth understanding rather than glossing over. In 2023 a federal judge in the Southern District of New York sanctioned lawyers who filed a brief relying on judicial decisions that did not exist, generated by a general-purpose AI chatbot. The court’s language in that case has been quoted repeatedly since: “A fake opinion is not ‘existing law’ and citation to a fake opinion does not provide a non-frivolous ground for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law, or for establishing new law. An attempt to persuade a court or oppose an adversary by relying on fake opinions is an abuse of the adversary system.”

A year later, the Second Circuit addressed the same conduct. There, an attorney admitted citing a nonexistent state court decision in a reply brief after a chatbot suggested it, and acknowledged she had not read or otherwise confirmed the decision. The court referred her to its Grievance Panel and stated the obligation in one sentence: “At the very least, the duties imposed by Rule 11 require that attorneys read, and thereby confirm the existence and validity of, the legal authorities on which they rely.” The court added that no new rule about AI was necessary to tell a licensed attorney that her submissions must be accurate.

Neither court said the technology is forbidden. Both said the person signing the document is responsible for verifying it, which has always been true. The defense against a fabricated citation is reading the actual source, and that is a human obligation that does not get delegated anywhere. Washington’s Rules of Professional Conduct point the same direction. RPC 3.3(a)(1) provides that a lawyer shall not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal, and a citation to an opinion that does not exist is a false statement of law whether or not the lawyer meant it.

sections.heading: What happens to your confidential information

paras.p: Clients should ask this more often than they do, because the answer varies enormously between offices. When a lawyer puts your facts into a software tool, those facts leave the office. Where they go, who can read them, whether they are retained, and whether they are used to train anything are all determined by the contract behind that tool, and plenty of lawyers have never read it. Washington RPC 1.6(a) prohibits revealing information relating to the representation without informed consent, and RPC 1.6(c) requires a lawyer to “make reasonable efforts to prevent the inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure of, or unauthorized access to, information relating to the representation of a client.” A free consumer chatbot with terms permitting the provider to use submitted content is a poor fit for that obligation.

Along the same lines, the competence rule reaches this. Comment 8 to Washington RPC 1.1 says a lawyer should keep abreast of changes in the law and its practice “including the benefits and risks associated with relevant technology.” Understanding where your file goes is part of the job rather than an optional extra.

sections.heading: The lawyer signs it, so the lawyer owns it

paras.p: There is no AI-related excuse available to the person who signs a filing. Washington RPC 5.3 makes a lawyer responsible for making reasonable efforts to ensure that the conduct of nonlawyer assistance is compatible with the lawyer’s own professional obligations, and responsible outright for conduct the lawyer orders or ratifies. Whatever a tool produces becomes the lawyer’s work product the moment it is adopted, and it carries the lawyer’s name, the lawyer’s judgment, and the lawyer’s exposure.
In practice that means every proposition in a document I file traces to a source I actually opened and read, rather than to a source a system told me about.

sections.heading: How AI should show up on your bill

paras.p: If a tool makes a task faster, the client should see that. The ABA Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility addressed generative AI in Formal Opinion 512 (2024), which works through the lawyer’s obligations on competence, confidentiality, candor to the tribunal, supervision, client communication, and fees. The fee point is the one clients care about: efficiency gained by a tool is not a basis for billing as though the slower method were still in use.

Correspondingly, Washington RPC 1.5(a) says a lawyer shall not make an agreement for, charge, or collect an unreasonable fee, and the first listed factor in the reasonableness analysis is the time and labor required. A lawyer who spends ninety seconds on something and bills two hours is not describing the time and labor required. Honest timekeeping is the whole answer here, and it is not complicated.

sections.heading: Four questions worth asking any lawyer

paras.p: Do you use AI in your practice, and for what? A confident lawyer will give you a specific answer. Vagueness or offense is itself informative.
Where does my information go, and what do the terms of that tool permit the provider to do with it? The lawyer should know, and should be able to tell you in plain words.
How do you verify legal citations before a document is filed? The right answer describes a process of reading the source, not a statement of trust in a tool.
If a tool saves you time, how does that appear on my invoice? You are entitled to ask, and the answer tells you most of what you need to know about how the office handles money.

sections.heading: How I use it

paras.p: I run an AI-assisted practice and I am direct about it, because the alternative is pretending otherwise. Software helps me read large record sets, organize discovery, produce first drafts, and check long documents for internal inconsistency. Every citation in anything I file is verified against the actual authority before it goes out, every document is reviewed and revised by me, and the strategic decisions in your matter are mine. The tooling makes me faster at the mechanical parts, and it does not form the theory of your case.

sections.heading: About my practice

paras.p: I am Justin D. Leigh, an independent attorney with an office in downtown Spokane. My practice covers civil litigation, employment and civil rights claims, real estate and land use, business and regulatory work including alcohol beverage licensing, estate planning and probate, and family law, and I appear in Spokane County Superior Court and throughout Eastern Washington. I am admitted in Washington (WSBA #55307) and Oregon (OSB #242384).

The reason I am willing to write this page is that the value of a lawyer was never the typing. It is knowing which facts matter, which argument to make, what a particular courtroom will do with it, and when to tell a client something they do not want to hear. No tool does any of that.

paras.p: I offer a free initial consultation by appointment at my downtown Spokane office. Questions about how a lawyer handles your information are reasonable to ask before you hire anyone, including me, and I would rather answer them early than have you wonder.
